Abstract---Head pose estimation and behavior recognition are fundamental yet difficult aspects of human analysis, especially when combined, as seen in our proposed HeadPoseAndBehavNet (HPABNet). This model employs a fully convolutional architecture designed to jointly estimate head poses and classify behaviors. To facilitate simultaneous training and evaluation, we developed an innovative dual-task loss function that addresses four key problems: (1) predicting roll, pitch, and yaw angles, (2) predicting a discrete head pose class, (3) predicting a discrete behavioral class, and (4) calculating an occlusion mask. During training, this loss guides the network to learn an initial model capable of solving all four issues. During inference, we compute an occlusion mask from the predicted roll and pitch angles to exclude head regions likely to be occluded; the remaining non-occluded features are then used to estimate head pose and behavior. Experimental results on two public datasets, AffectNet and GOHPP (University of Alberta), indicate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art solutions. Notably, occlusion handling was integrated into a single model alongside pose and behavior estimation, unlike other approaches that require separate models for occlusion masking. The code is accessible at https://github.com/headposeandbehavnet/HPABNet.

Although this phenomenon is often blamed on forecasting inaccuracies or operational breakdowns, we argue it stems from risk-averse scheduling strategies. By applying a stochastic self-scheduling model to real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, we show that risk-averse storage units adopt a short-sighted operational approach. Specifically, they focus primarily on near-term price arbitrage, targeting only a limited number of extreme price peaks and valleys, which leaves them inactive during many periods characterized by significantly high or low prices. These findings carry significant policy weight, particularly given the lack of transparency surrounding unit-level risk aversion and the visible risks involved in intervention decisions. Consequently, regulators utilizing unit-based models to assess market outcomes may struggle to resolve issues related to stored electricity displacement. To address this, we suggest enhancing policy models through the introduction of a fictional storage entity representing the aggregate storage capacity. This proposed unit would operate with aggressive risk-seeking behavior, effectively mimicking a warehouse that buys at any price below a high threshold and sells at any price exceeding a low threshold. Our results indicate that replacing actual storage units with this fictional unit in market unit commitment models would likely exacerbate any existing tendencies towards stored electricity dispatch. Ultimately, we contend that the challenge of stored electricity dispatch will persist as long as real-world storage units continue their unitary, risk-averse scheduling practices. We conclude by suggesting potential monitoring metrics and regulatory interventions, such as table sales and hook-up payments, designed to encourage more aggressive risk-taking and reduce the risk of short-sighted storage unit behavior.

Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. Additionally, a regular baroclinic wave regime appears at intermediate thermal Rossby numbers, with its characteristics and dominant zonal wavenumber heavily influenced by radiative and frictional damping strengths. These regular waves display notable similarities to baroclinic storms observed on Mars under specific conditions. At the highest rotation rates, multiple jets develop when the Rossby deformation radius and other eddy-related scales are significantly smaller than the planetary radius; these resemble the multiple zonal jets found on gas giant planets. These jets form on scales comparable to the most energetic eddies, poleward of the supercritical latitude, near the Rhines scale. Finally, the balance of forces acting on these multiple jets is examined by analyzing the budget of zonal momentum. The study concludes by summarizing the key similarities and differences between the University of Hamburg GCM's results and those of more complex models featuring realistic physics and boundary conditions. These multiple zonal jets are also documented in idealized models featuring rotating tanks with stratified fluids on a $\beta$-plane, as well as on rapidly rotating gas giants, Mars, and Jupiter/Saturn. This research adds value by detailing the dependent scaling laws of these multiple jets regarding rotational and thermal forcing, their length scales, and the balance of zonal momentum. These multiple jets always form beyond the scale of the Rossby deformation radius or the Rhines scale, arising from the interaction between the eddy kinetic energy cascade and planetary rotation. AL is particularly valuable in large-scale industrial applications where labeling expenses are high, prompting practitioners to utilize every available technique to enhance model accuracy. The recent achievements of self-supervised pretraining (SSP) underscore the significance of leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled data to improve model outcomes. In this study, we investigate the combination of AL and SSP using ImageNet. We observe that performance on small toy datasets—the standard benchmark in current literature—does not accurately reflect performance on ImageNet, as active learners tend to select class-imbalanced samples. Among the existing baselines tested, popular AL algorithms across various small and large-scale settings fail to surpass random sampling. To address the issue of class imbalance, we introduce Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward and scalable AL algorithm that consistently outperforms random sampling by choosing more balanced samples for scale. Our results indicate that the underperformance of current methods stems from the inadequacy of existing evaluation frameworks. Finally, we reveal through a case study that the choice of loss function and label smoothing are critical factors in the successful application of AL. Formulating DP for graphs is challenging because data points are interconnected, often in non-linear or sparse ways, which complicates calculating individual privacy loss in differentially private learning. This difficulty is intensified by the lack of a single, established DP framework for graph settings, a problem that extends to GNNs and makes private machine learning on such data particularly difficult. Motivated by the absence of prior systematic research, we analyze graph-based learning from a privacy standpoint. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even at short wavelengths. Based on this framework, we formulate a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme that extends the simulation duration for non-equilibrium scenarios beyond the limits of the full positive-P method, though this involves approximating quantum fluctuations. We demonstrate that this linearized scheme aligns directly with established Bogoliubov methods. Additionally, we validate the utility and benefits of this formalism by investigating correlations in a quantum shock wave scenario and contrasting its predictions with other standard quantum many-body approaches. The formalism is designed to be readily adaptable to other problems, such as analyzing post-quench dynamics in sudden quantum phase transitions. More broadly, the presented framework offers significant potential for studying intricate correlations in the context of the 1D unitary Bose gas.

Quantum fluids of interacting bosons exhibit rich and varied behaviors that can be investigated through both weakly interacting gas models and strongly interacting unitary limits. We examine how quantum correlations in the dense phase following a beam-like quantum shock wave align with predictions from Landau-Hidakae dynamics. This scenario serves as a direct test of the model's capacity to capture essential quantum characteristics, as it involves the interaction of two independent quantum velocities of the gas. We demonstrate that, in this specific case, the predictions of our model match those of the GPE-Wigner method, a standard technique in quantum hydrodynamics used to simulate the full many-body wavefunction. These findings validate the application of positive-P methods to determine key properties of quantum correlations in unitary Bose gases. Our results underscore the value of these simulations in deepening our understanding of quantum fluid dynamics, particularly regarding the formation of quantum vortex arrays in two-dimensional superfluids. The computational code implementing this work will be made publicly available.

However, we establish that a local quadratic isoperimetric inequality holds for maps that are relatively 1-homotopic. Under the assumption of non-positive curvature, the exponent of this inequality can be optimized to 1.

used technique for evaluating machine learning models, facilitating both model selection and parameter optimization. However, because CV relies on random data partitioning, the resulting performance estimates are stochastic and can exhibit significant variability, particularly in natural language processing (NLP). We show that such unstable estimates are unsuitable for effective parameter tuning; consequently, the selected parameters are highly sensitive to data splits, often leading to sub-optimal choices and severe reproducibility challenges.

To address this, we propose employing J-K-fold CV, which utilizes J independent K-fold cross-validations to assess performance. Our primary contributions involve extending J-K-fold CV to the domain of parameter tuning and exploring strategies for selecting optimal values for J and K. We argue that minimizing variability is more critical than reducing bias for successful tuning, advocating for lower-than-typical values of K in NLP literature. This allows computational resources to be redirected toward increasing J. To validate the broad applicability of our recommendations, we examine a diverse set of case studies, including sentiment classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging, and document classification. Our findings offer practical, evidence-based guidance for designing J-K-fold CV to optimize both cost and performance when tuning parameters in NLP.

To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were initially introduced in the context of knowledge distillation, enabling lightweight student networks to match the performance of complex teacher models. Finally, we explore future research directions concerning architecture design, knowledge quality, and theoretical advancements in regression-based learning. By providing a thorough overview, this survey offers valuable insights and practical guidelines for both industry professionals and the academic community regarding Teacher-Student architectures in multi-objective knowledge learning.

Notably, the sizeable photon-recoil shift imposes fundamental limits on the short-term frequency stability of the Sr narrow-line clock and the precision of absorption measurements. We propose that these abrupt shear-thickening events serve as precursors to a rigidity transition and present a comprehensive theory of viscosity based on a universal crossover scaling function that bridges the frictionless jamming point with a rigidity transition induced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Experimental validation using two distinct systems—cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol—demonstrates that viscosity data collapse onto a single universal curve across a broad spectrum of stresses and volume fractions. This collapse identifies two separate scaling regimes characterized by different critical exponents, confirming that frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming belong to distinct universality classes. By incorporating material-specific microscale interactions into a scaling variable that governs proximity to shear jamming (dependent on both stress and volume fraction), this reformulation enables the application of established theoretical frameworks for equilibrium critical phenomena to uncover the fundamental physics of the shear thickening transition. Consequently, this approach facilitates more accurate predictions of flow behavior in dense suspensions and offers a pathway to control their rheological properties.

Since the initial discovery of shear thickening in carbon-black oils nearly eight decades ago, abrupt viscosity jumps in suspensions have been linked to the onset of rigidity in various theoretical models. However, existing theories either focus exclusively on frictionless particulate frameworks without accounting for polydispersity or assume monodisperse particles while incorporating frictional contacts, yet they fail to capture the complete microscale complexity of real materials. This study investigates the microscopic origins of these abrupt transitions through direct local measurements of particle-level microstructure and contact forces in sheared cornstarch-in-glycerol suspensions. The results indicate that polydispersity significantly influences the microscale physics of shear thickening. Specifically, cornstarch suspensions exhibit two distinct types of sudden viscosity increases governed by critical exponents different from those of frictionless particulate matter. These exponents align with a universality class defined by a rigid particulate state characterized by strong anisotropic interactions. This finding underscores that the microscale physics of shear thickening in frictional particulate suspensions is intrinsically tied to the emergence of long-range anisotropic interactions. Furthermore, the direct observation of local microstructure prior to sudden viscosity leaps provides concrete evidence of a rigidity transition and reveals how polydispersity alters the associated critical exponents.

This study examines how public sector officials evaluate their reliance on Google, their awareness of algorithmic biases affecting information retrieval, and the extent of relevant data potentially lost due to personalization. Our experimental results reveal that most participants are unaware of these risks and lack strategies to mitigate the possibility of missing crucial information. Most notably, we present empirical evidence suggesting that personalization can cause the omission of up to 20% of relevant information. Consequently, this research underscores the need for public sector professionals to receive training on algorithmic biases that influence decision-making and to follow clear guidelines for minimizing the risk of overlooking pertinent data during online searches. To achieve this, we offer practical recommendations for maintaining the recall of relevant information, such as performing a final search without enabling personalization features. This work advances prior efforts by providing the first quantitative demonstration of how search result recall is impacted by personalization. Search engines significantly influence how public sector officials locate and utilize information, yet there is concern that algorithmic biases and personalization could lead to missing critical data. While we show that document recall can decrease by as much as 20% in certain scenarios, our findings also indicate that personalization rarely (0–2%) reduces recall below 80%. These results empower practitioners to make informed decisions regarding potential risks of lost relevant information and confirm that search engineers can often rely on personalized results while maintaining high recall levels. Furthermore, we observe that recall degradation varies across queries, often stemming from duplicate content issues where the top personalized result fails to rank alongside other duplicates. Leveraging this insight, we recommend a straightforward strategy to prevent recall loss: conduct a final search devoid of personalization. This can be seamlessly integrated into standard workflows, such as copying and pasting the gathered information into a new tab for a personalization-free search. Our findings are based on a controlled lab study involving public sector officials and an automated analysis of query logs from a major Canadian government website. We conclude that officials should be aware of how search engine biases impact retrieval and that organizations can adopt the recommended recall-minimizing strategies. We further provide guidance on implementing this approach within existing workflows and discuss its benefits, limitations, and trade-offs. Personalization in web search increasingly affects how public sector professionals locate and employ information; however, the consequences of algorithmic biases on decision-making and the potential for missing critical data remain largely theoretical. **Approach:** Continuous k-space data were collected using a rewound Cartesian acquisition with spiral profile ordering (rCASPR). This method was designed to match the contrast of conventional linear phase encoding while organizing data into multiple respiratory phases. Low-resolution, respiratory-correlated 4D images were reconstructed via compressed sensing to estimate non-rigid deformation vector fields, which facilitated motion-compensated image reconstruction. The rCASPR sampling technique was compared against linear and CASPR sampling regarding point-spread function (PSF) and image contrast through in silico, phantom, and in vivo studies. A grid search was employed to determine optimal reconstruction parameters for low-resolution 4D-MRI, specifically spatial resolution and temporal regularization. The proposed motion-compensated rCASPR was tested in eight healthy volunteers and benchmarked against free-breathing scans utilizing linear sampling, with image quality assessed both visually and quantitatively using gradient entropy.

**Findings:** rCASPR demonstrated a superior PSF (comparable in ky but narrower in kz) with no significant difference in image contrast relative to linear sampling. Optimal 4D-MRI reconstruction parameters were identified as a spatial resolution of $4.5 \text{ mm}^3$ and a temporal regularization value of $0.003$. Consequently, the mean gradient entropy in lung tissue decreased by $30.4\%$ post-reconstruction compared to pre-reconstruction levels. Finally, MR-guidance was tested on a phantom with linear linear motion, showing successful signal localization within a $3 \text{ mm}$ tolerance of the actual position.

**Conclusion:** rCASPR is a viable sampling method for free-breathing 4D-MRI, enabling retrospective image reconstruction across multiple respiratory phases. Successful MR-guidance validation in phantoms and the substantial reduction in breathing artifacts (evidenced by lower gradient entropy) confirm successful motion estimation and compensation. These motion-compensated 4D $T_2$-weighted images offer enhanced anatomical detail, making them valuable for tracking structures of clinical interest, such as the prostate in patients with pelvic pathologies or lungs in cancer therapy planning and monitoring. However, practitioners have historically relied on Monte Carlo approximations because no suitable exact algorithm existed. This paper introduces an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test applicable to a specific family of structured test statistics. The proposed algorithm operates in $\mathcal{O}(GN (\log GN )(\log N ))$ time, where $N$ represents the dataset size and $G$ denotes the range of the test statistic. Experimental results indicate that our exact algorithm is 10 times faster than a Monte Carlo approximation using 20,000 samples on a standard dataset. We further apply this algorithm to re-examine significant claims from prior work suggesting that neural networks outperform heuristic NLP systems, observing in one instance a reduction from a p-value of 0.05 to exactly zero. To facilitate future research, we have open-sourced the algorithm through the NLPTests Python package. We urge practitioners to replace current Monte Carlo approaches with our efficient exact algorithm and to leverage the implemented multiple testing corrections to determine which performance metric gaps are truly significant. Our algorithm achieves its optimal time complexity when the test statistic takes integer values within a known range $[0, G]$; otherwise, the complexity becomes $\mathcal{O}(GN (\log GN )(\log (GN ))$. These results represent a significant advancement over the current best approximate algorithm, which requires $\mathcal{O}(GN (\log N ))$ time.

Rising inflation rates have driven individuals to shift funds from savings into stocks, commodities, and other investment avenues. Deep Learning models have repeatedly demonstrated their efficacy in forecasting time series data. Consequently, technical analysis utilizing various indicators remains a standard practice for traders and investors. Additionally, sentiment analysis gauges investor emotions and their propensity to invest. Globally, practitioners have employed diverse techniques ranging from basic Machine Learning to advanced Neural Networks, experimenting with methods from simple linear regression to complex architectures to predict market movements. Recent events clearly illustrate the impact of news and headlines on stock markets and cryptocurrencies. This paper introduces an ensemble of cutting-edge methods for stock price prediction. Specifically, it performs sentiment analysis on news and headlines concerning Apple Inc. (NASDAQ) using BERT, a pre-trained transformer model for Natural Language Processing. Subsequently, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) forecasts Apple Inc.'s stock price by integrating technical indicators, global stock indices, commodity prices, historical data, and sentiment scores. The proposed approach is benchmarked against baseline models, including Long Short Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), vanilla GANs, and the Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms baselines in prediction accuracy, particularly during periods of heightened news and headline activity. This study underscores the critical role of event-driven news and current affairs in stock market forecasting. To access the Python code, please visit the following link: https://github.com/Rohit1610/Stock_Price_Prediction. Future research could adapt this framework for predicting the prices of cryptocurrencies or other highly volatile assets.

We begin by analyzing the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) before comparing our results with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our analysis starts with the primary subprocess driving the total cross section, $e^+e^- \to HH \nu \bar \nu$, known as vector boson fusion ($WW \to HH$). We provide a comprehensive examination of the cross section $\sigma(W_X W_Y\to HH)$ as a function of subprocess energy for both EFTs, covering all polarization combinations ($LL, TT, LT, TL$) and the most pertinent effective operators. We demonstrate that within the HEFT framework, the total cross section is entirely accounted for by the $LL$ contribution, which at TeV energies is predominantly governed by two specific HEFT coefficients. By matching the scattering amplitudes between the two EFTs for this subprocess, we establish the correspondence between the leading coefficients in HEFT and SMEFT. Finally, we assess the sensitivity to these two dominant HEFT coefficients at CLIC (3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$). We conclude by delineating the accessible parameter space for these coefficients, based on the full dataset from each machine, under the assumption of no other significant contributions. With the high luminosity available at these future colliders, precise measurements of the total cross section and its polarization-dependent components will enable tests of new physics through the analysis of a small subset of effective operators. Along the way, we present a collection of scattering amplitudes in both EFTs, featuring a novel application of the Unitary Gauge for heavy vector bosons within an EFT context, along with relevant computational code. We also offer insights into the magnitude of radiative corrections arising from the large mass of the $Z'$ boson in this specific process. Alongside standard references, we highlight pertinent literature on related topics, including the SMEFT-Higgs code and the HELAS library. This work serves as a follow-up to our earlier analysis of the simpler subprocess $e^+e^- \to HH Z Z$. This process begins with a specific parametrization of the geometry, termed 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization, which reformulates general relativity to facilitate an analytical $1/c^2$ expansion. As a result, we derive the expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action up to the next-to-next-to-leading order. Additionally, an appendix provides the derivation of post-non-relativistic expansions for the Ricci scalar and the $\sqrt{-g}$ term. The findings from this study are intended to support the derivation of the Bernoulli equation for gravity, as previously outlined in reference [1]. Our results will likewise assist in obtaining the next-to-next-to-order terms in the $1/c^2$ expansion of the Bernoulli equation of gravity, an project previously undertaken by our research group. This endeavor is significant for formulating a consistent effective field theory of non-relativistic gravity [2–11].

Since its introduction [12–14], the Bernoulli equation of gravity has been a pivotal tool in various domains, including the study of black hole evaporation [15–22], cosmological inflation [23–29], gravitational wave generation [30–34], and the holographic principle [35–42]. Furthermore, extending the effective field theory of non-relativistic gravity [43–49] beyond next-to-leading order requires the second order in the $1/c^2$ expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action. Consequently, the current work is essential for advancing that specific project. Additionally, similar $1/c^2$ expansion techniques can be applied to the Purdy action [50–52], as explored in references [53, 54].

While the derivation of the post-Newtonian expansion of the Einstein equations is a well-established achievement [55–70], the corresponding post-Newtonian expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action remains less developed. Relevant studies in this area include [71–79]. In contrast to the post-Newtonian framework, our $1/c^2$ expansion scheme shares common ground with the Bernoulli equation of gravity. This similarity arises because both approaches model spacetime as divided into 'fast' regions, governed by relativistic physics, and 'slow' regions, governed by non-relativistic physics

intruder with length $L$ and diameter $D$ moving through water-saturated granular beds at a fixed depth. Using polystyrene and hydrogel grains with diameter $d$, we examine materials exhibiting high and negligible contact friction, respectively. Drag forces were measured for orientations both perpendicular ($F_\perp$) and parallel ($F_\parallel$) to the cylinder's axis across a range of speeds $U$, spanning from quasi-static to rate-dependent regimes. Results indicate that the drag anisotropy ratio, $\xi = F_\perp/F_\parallel$, is not constant but rises substantially with both the driving rate and the aspect ratio $L/D$ in both granular media. Specifically, for $L/D = 40$, $\xi$ increases from 2.2 to 2.8 in high-friction beds and from 4.0 to 4.6 in low-friction beds as the nondimensional Froude number $Fr = U/\sqrt{g(D+d)}$ varies between $10^{-4}$ and $2 \times 10^{-2}$. On average, $\xi$ exhibits a logarithmic increase with $L/D$ when $L/D \gg 1$. Leveraging the log-law structure of fluid drag, we propose a rescaling of $\xi$ based on a granular friction Reynolds number ${\cal R}e_\gamma$ and a contact-friction analog of the Karman constant, which aligns data for both materials. Additionally, we analyze the origin of drag anisotropy in terms of active force transmission and reorganize existing scaling laws for $\xi$ using the dimensionless depth $\zeta = h/d$. Ultimately, we discuss these findings in the context of the aspect-ratio-dependent transition from rolling to tipping motion. This research offers insights into the dynamics of objects embedded in granular environments, an phenomenon prevalent in diverse natural and industrial contexts.

There is a well-established history of analyzing and creating structure-preserving discretization methods, ranging from proving that standard schemes retain these properties to designing novel high-order schemes that exactly preserve them. However, when combined with implicit time-stepping, a significant drawback is that these properties typically depend on solving the potentially nonlinear systems of equations exactly at each time step. While feasible for small systems within floating-point precision, this approach becomes impractical for the large linear systems encountered in typical space-time PDE discretizations. This paper introduces a modification to the standard flexible generalized minimum residual (FGMRES) iteration that imposes selected constraints on approximate numerical solutions. We illustrate its effectiveness by applying it to both conservation law systems and dissipative systems. Most existing literature assumes that the nonlinear system solver preserves key properties of the continuous problem at every time step. By providing accurate iterative solutions that maintain these properties, our proposed approach reduces the burden on nonlinear solvers and may lower the overall computational cost. Existing solvers can readily incorporate this framework as long as the system residuals satisfy the necessary structural constraints. Existing constraints have already been implemented for popular codes, such as those found in OpenFOAM and COMSOL, although they were originally developed for steady-state problems. We begin by outlining the general approach and its theoretical foundations, followed by applications to specific PDE systems. First, we address systems of non-linear hyperbolic equations, demonstrating how to impose discrete conservation of mass, momentum, and energy. Second, we consider the Navier-Stokes equations showing how to maintain both conservation of mass and the maximum-principle for density. Finally, we generalize the approach to handle additional properties, such as the discrete entropy inequality for compressible flow. Our numerical experiments indicate that this method can significantly reduce computational expense. Specifically, we observe a speedup of up to a factor of four for 3D incompressible flow simulations and even greater reductions for high-Mach-number compressible flow simulations when using FGMRES with our proposed constraints. We conclude by suggesting potential extensions to other time-stepping schemes.

This process involves aligning a preoperative CT-derived organ model with an intraoperative surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. The task is complex due to factors such as sparse and noisy real-time data, numerous unknowns regarding tissue properties and boundary conditions, and the difficulty of establishing correspondences between pre- and intraoperative datasets. These challenges are exacerbated by the liver's lack of distinct surface features and the disparate noise characteristics of the imaging modalities used. To address this, we developed a convolutional neural network that simultaneously performs surface correspondence search and non-rigid registration. The network was trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly generated, deforming organ-like structures, enabling immediate generalization to new patients without retraining. Originating in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, the investigation of graphs with the PMH-property integrates three fundamental graph concepts: matchings, Hamiltonicity, and edge-colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs, aiming to characterize those where every perfect matching aligns with a specific colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. We demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to the graphs being even-2-factorable (E2F), meaning all their 2-factors consist exclusively of even cycles. While bipartite cubic graphs trivially satisfy the E2F property, our analysis is restricted to non-bipartite cubic graphs. Although the PMH-property provides a sufficient (though not necessary) condition for a cubic graph to be E2F, the primary objective of this work is to define an infinite family of non-bipartite, E2F cubic graphs parameterized by two variables, which we term "papillon graphs." We further determine the specific parameter values under which these papillon graphs exhibit the PMH-property or are merely E2F, and we prove that papillon graphs with distinct parameters are never isomorphic. Additionally, our analysis reveals that papillon graphs are Hamiltonian if and only if their parameter $y$ is even; when $y$ is even, they decompose into three 1-factors. The paper concludes by examining whether generalizations of papillon graphs can yield cubic graphs with the PMH-property that are not E2F, and we discuss potential characterization conditions for E2F cubic graphs that extend beyond the papillon family. Wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) alleviates the requirement for strict adherence to the physical wave equation during iterations, whereas extended source waveform inversion (ESI) employs a non-physical source distributed across the computational domain that iteratively migrates toward the true physical source. Both WRI and ESI operate within a shared mathematical framework utilizing the Lagrangian-based adjoint-state method, with a specific emphasis on time-domain formulations using extended sources. Conceptually, WRI and ESI can be regarded as weighted variants of classical FWI. First, we demonstrate that employing a single extended source positioned at the array center yields superior imaging results at deep interfaces compared to array-center imaging at shallow depths when utilizing a global ESI formulation; conversely, a shallow extended source placement proves most effective for medium-depth imaging. Second, distributing multiple extended sources uniformly along the array axis and combining them into a combined ESI formulation offers advantages over both single and standard multi-source setups. Our numerical model employs a 2D elastic medium featuring a velocity jump at the surface and a salt dome obstacle. Wavefield reconstruction serves as a validation tool for these formulations, and we explicitly address issues regarding the determination of extended source amplitude. These sources can be strategically deployed to mitigate concerns about local minima and array coverage limitations. Ultimately, we contend that such sources are most effective when their combined ESI formulation is employed and that their application is particularly beneficial in scenarios involving large velocity contrasts, extensive data arrays, or data gaps caused by the ocean or topography.

In this system, one species can invade only nearest-neighbor sites, whereas the other species can invade sites at any distance but possesses lower local competitiveness, establishing with a probability $g \le 1$. Specifically, for sub-GeV particles, the combination of $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ at Belle II and beam-dump experiments offers the greatest sensitivity, whereas for heavier particles, the smallest couplings can be probed through the detection of two-body decays alone. Consequently, the future sensitivity to the parameter space of two-body decays $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ will be determined by the combination of signals from $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ reconstruction and beam-dump missing energy searches. Our theory demonstrates that these fluids can maintain coherent motion, characterized by a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit, despite the disruptive effects of the disorder. Nevertheless, linearized hydrodynamics fails to capture the scaling behavior of these active systems in spatial dimensions ranging from 2 to 5. This study presents a robust method for modeling the transport of nutrients, chemicals, or waste products by incompressible polar active fluids with quenched disorder, ensuring their correct advection while accounting for diffusive effects and spatially varying order parameter exponents. We also examine the emergence of symmetry breaking in the advection-diffusion equation and verify that our derived dimension-dependent scaling exponents for spatially homogeneous systems align with existing literature findings on these exponents. Additionally, we confirm that these exponents are identical for both conservative and dissipative active matter. However, when a driving force is introduced, the system undergoes a phase transition, and the symmetry-breaking exponent assumes a value of 5/3, consistent with previous studies on active matter in this dimension. Furthemore, we illustrate how these phenomena can be observed in experimental or simulations involving swarming bacteria or swimming microorganisms. Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect, a net torque generated by the reflection and thermal re-emission of solar radiation from their surfaces. This phenomenon causes a gradual alteration in rotation periods, which is most readily observable in light curves due to the quadratic accumulation of phase shifts over time. We gathered archived light curves and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids (10115) 1992 SK, (1620) Geographos, and (1685) Toro. Using light curve inversion, we fitted the data to convex shape models, modeling the YORP effect as a linear variation in rotation frequency ($\upsilon \equiv \mathrm{d}\omega / \mathrm{d}t$) and optimizing it alongside other spin and shape parameters. For asteroid (10115) 1992 SK, we detected a rotational acceleration of $\upsilon = (8.3 \pm 0.6) \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, which aligns well with theoretical predictions for its specific shape and spin model. Regarding (1685) Toro, we measured $\upsilon = (3.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, a value closer to zero than previous findings, which may indicate that Toro's spin state has approached the YORP equilibrium. For asteroid (1620) Geographos, our result $\upsilon = (-1.3 \pm 0.6) \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$ contradicts earlier reports, potentially stemming from differences in the assumed convex shape model. We note that the interpretation of the YORP effect for asteroids with non-convex shapes, such as Geographos and 1992 SK, remains uncertain. To accurately determine the YORP acceleration for such bodies, one must disentangle the signal from other light curve variations, including those arising from surface inhomogeneities, which could ultimately refine our constraints on the effect. Our results for (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro represent the first measurements of YORP acceleration derived from light curves.

When restricted to the one-way model, these transducers characterize rational functions. Despite the robust characterization of regular functions by various finite-state devices, even the subclass of rational functions may include functions that are not computable by a Turing machine with infinite input. This paper introduces a decision procedure for the synthesis problem: given a regular function $f$ (specified by one of the aforementioned transducer models), determine if $f$ is computable, and if so, construct a Turing machine that computes it. For regular functions, we demonstrate that computability is equivalent to continuity, thereby reducing the problem to deciding continuity. We provide a generic characterization of continuity for functions that preserve regular languages under inverse image, such as regular functions, and utilize this to prove the decidability of continuity (and consequently computability) for both rational and regular functions. For rational functions, we show that this decision can be made in $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ (previously established as $\mathsf{PTime}$ by Prieur). Similarly, we effectively characterize the uniform continuity of regular functions and connect it to the concept of uniform computability, which provides stronger efficiency assurances. Additionally, we define and investigate the subclass of locally computable functions, demonstrating its relevance in algorithm design for regular functions. Deciding whether a regular function is locally computable is at least as hard as deciding regular function equality; however, we establish that it belongs to $\mathsf{DTime}(n^{3})$. This complexity bound follows from the fact that regular function equality lies in $\mathsf{NLogSpace$, a result achieved through the work of Thomas and later refined by/Prieur. Our findings extend to regular transductions (which are not necessarily functional). We also present related work on the complexity of regular transduction equality and algorithm construction, the decidability of algorithm equivalence for finite state strategies in repeated games, and the characterization of continuous functions from infinite sequences to infinite sequences. Deciding the computability of a regular function relies on verifying the continuity of the corresponding transduction; this involves checking the uniform continuity of the minimal 1-reversible transducer representing the function, a problem solved via the method of "virtual miniestimates," which can be decided in $\mathsf{NLogSpace$.

surrogate models of dynamical systems, achieving this with fewer trainable parameters and less training data compared to other methods. A simplified variant, called next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), further streamlines the algorithm by eliminating the need to tune the training data scale. This study examines the training process of both RC and NGRC on dynamical systems exhibiting symmetry-breaking behavior. The results indicate that the order parameter during NGRC training follows a sequence of symmetry-breaking patterns similar to the Benmerad instability. Additionally, NGRC training is identified as a source of time-reversal symmetry breaking, a phenomenon also observed during the training of ordinary RC computers. These findings suggest that symmetry-breaking order can emerge from the simplified dynamics of next-generation reservoir computing. During training, the input data scale becomes self-tuned; because this scale acts as a key control parameter for symmetry-breaking in physical systems, the order parameter of that symmetry-breaking process can serve as a probe to verify the next-generation RC hypothesis. The Benmerad instability is notably simple, occurring in a system with a complex order parameter defined by two variables: a magnitude (similar to the RC output scale) and a phase (related to time translation symmetry). The order parameter's evolution during training reflects the competition between the input data scale and the time scale of the target time series. This paper provides the equations of motion for the Benmerad instability and explores the parameter dependencies of its various phases, including descriptions of two time-crystal phases that feature competing time-displacement symmetries and a period-doubling bifurcation. Furthermore, the study analyzes the relationship between the NGRC training dynamics and time-crystal phenomena found in other reservoir computing variants. Ultimately, the paper argues that the core mechanism of reservoir computer training involves symmetry breaking and the emergence of an order parameter, a principle that extends beyond RC to other machine learning algorithms. The Benmerad instability is presented as a simplified, canonical model for understanding this broader phenomenon. Assuming sufficient regularity and continuity of the HJI partial differential equation across the state space, we demonstrate that, under state feedback control against worst-case disturbances, this method enables the computation of the reachable state set within a specified verification time horizon. Within a finite time horizon defined by the verification time, we show that the reachable set corresponds to the state- and input-constrained minimum time set, equivalent to a standard reachability problem. Our approach utilizes an explicit numerical scheme to solve the associated second-order Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation within a fixed time step framework. To date, this represents the first instance of solving a second-order HJB equation with state feedback and worst-case disturbances to determine the reachable state set. While second-order terms are typically employed to elucidate boundary conditions, we leverage them to calculate gradients of the reachability function exclusively along the frontier of the reachable state set. By restricting the domain of the reachability function to the verification time horizon, we derive a boundary condition necessary for state feedback to execute within a finite horizon. This state feedback ensures the uniqueness of the reachability function, which is then employed to derive the reachable state set. We validate the efficacy and scalability of this methodology through a set of standard benchmark problems. Notably, using a third-order explicit scheme, we achieve a 100-fold increase in resolution (grid size) compared to the conventional scheme state of the art, and a 200-fold increase when accounting for computational time, all while maintaining high accuracy. Second-order schemes are inherently susceptible to numerical instabilities; however, we mitigate this by periodically resetting the reachability function, an technique we generalize to apply to any boundary condition. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach to determine the reachable state set from the state- and input-constrained minimum time function, differing from existing methods. We analyze the key components of our solution, including the boundary condition, the restriction of the search to the reachable state set, and the explicit numerical scheme, to provide insights for future scalability enhancements. We also outline a framework for evaluating the reachability of invariant sets. Although developed for deterministic HJI problems, the proposed solution structure is adaptable to stochastic settings. In this study, we tested both theories using a stimulus set where visual categorizability and agency were dissociated, based on convolutional neural network representations and behavioral data. fMRI results revealed that visual categorizability and agency account for independent components of the animacy continuum in VTC; when modeled together, they fully explain the continuum. This paper generalizes the concept of codiskcyclicity, originally defined for a single operator $T \in L(X)$, to a set of operators $\Gamma \subset L(X)$. We derive several key results regarding codiskcyclic operator sets and formulate a corresponding criterion for codiskcyclicity. Furthermore, as an application, we investigate the codiskcyclicity of $C_0$-semigroups. It is established that a $C_0$-semigroup $U(\cdot)$ on $X$ is codiskcyclic if and only if its generator $A$ is codiskcyclic; in such cases, the semigroup fails to be strongly continuous on any disk $\{z \in X : |z| < \rho\}$ for any $\rho > 0$, unless the space $X$ reduces to the trivial $\{0\}$. Additionally, we examine the codiskcyclicity of operator sets form $X$ to $Y$, where both $X$ and $Y$ are Banach algebras. Specifically, let $A \subset X$ and $B \subset Y$ be open sets containing the scalars $\{0\}$. An operator tuple $\mathcal{T} = (T_a : a \in A)$ from $X$ to $Y$ is termed codiskcyclic if, for every non-zero $x \in X$, the orbit map $a \mapsto T_a(x)$ is injective and its image is dense within the set $\{T_a(y) : y \in B, a \in A\}$. Consequently, no such codiskcyclic tuple can exist when restricted to open neighborhoods of $\{0\}$ in either $X$ or $Y$. As an application, we demonstrate that there does not exist a non-trivial codiskcyclic tuple composed of bounded analytic functions on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ from a Banach algebra $X$ to a Banach algebra $Y$. This finding extends the results of Gelfand (1940) and Lakshmikanth (1968). These discoveries were also established by S. Saha in his Ph.D. thesis at the University of North Bengal.

While prior research has established the existence of this issue, our work conducts novel investigations to quantify the bias, identify its root causes, and propose mitigation strategies. First, we establish quantitative metrics to measure $B_{\perp}$ bias across both local physical components and native image-plane components. We encourage the community to apply the quick fix where necessary and to employ the established quantitative metrics for assessing the severity of bias in their own outputs. Vector magnetic field observations are essential for understanding solar atmospheric physics and the associated storage and release of magnetic energy. Measuring the line-of-sight perpendicular component ($B_z$ or $B_{\perp}$) is crucial for accurately determining the total magnetic flux, the magnetic fill fraction ($ff$), the helicity content, and the available magnetic energy. Despite extensive efforts to derive $B_z$ via various inversion techniques, several studies have shown that the solution often suffers from bias, a problem exacerbated by the under-resolved nature of many magnetic structures. This paper seeks to enhance the cross-task generalization capabilities of large-scale multi-task language models, such as T0 and FLAN, within an unsupervised framework. We introduce ReCross, a retrieval-augmentation approach that utilizes a few unlabeled examples as queries to fetch a targeted subset of upstream data, thereby updating the model to improve its generalization performance. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed to synthesize structured data, such as knowledge graphs (KGs), knowledge tables (KTs), and knowledge graphs in code (KGC). However, current methods often produce inaccuracies and fail to generalize effectively when handling real-world natural language data. To address these limitations, we propose CrossKG, a framework for knowledge graph construction that leverages the multi-head attention mechanisms of LLMs to retrieve and integrate structured knowledge. CrossKG dynamically adapts the number of retrieved knowledge instances based on specific needs and captioning difficulties, ensuring an optimal balance between accuracy and generalization. We validated the framework's effectiveness and efficiency across three distinct knowledge tables and one knowledge graph in code. Our results show that CrossKG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios involving out-of-distribution entities and complex SQL queries. Additionally, our analysis provides insights into the integration of multiple knowledge sources and the utilization of attention heads for cross-domain knowledge construction. CrossKG is accessible at https://github.com/ali-zhang-yue/CrossKG.

Extending prior research, we fit median [X/Mg] versus [Mg/H] trends using a two-process model that separates abundance patterns into a "prompt" component linked to core-collapse supernovae and a "delayed" component associated with Type Ia supernovae. For individual stars, we determine the amplitudes of these two components and calculate residuals, denoted as \Delta[X/H], from the resulting two-parameter fit. The root-mean-square residuals span approximately 0.01–0.03 dex for the most precise APOGEE measurements, rising to about 0.1 dex for Na, V, and Ce. Correlation analyses of these residuals expose a complex underlying structure, featuring a correlated group of Ca, Na, Al, K, Ce, and Co, alongside a distinct group comprising Li, Cr, Mn, Ni, Cu, Zn, and Pb. Identifying stars that are outliers in these residual measurements can flag anomalous populations, such as open or globular clusters, or stars influenced by nucleosynthetic processes other than the primary and intermediate mass scenarios. Consequently, this straightforward and efficient analysis method serves as a superior alternative to complex spectral fitting techniques for diagnosing the abundance patterns of large numbers of Milky Way disk stars. The approach is readily adaptable to future surveys, such as the anticipated 4 million-star APOGEE program. We also present a Python package, dualAbundances, which facilitates the application of our analysis to new data.

-19 pandemic rapidly spread globally, causing severe repercussions in China. During this period, online rumors heightened public anxiety regarding health and social stability, making the detection and containment of such misinformation an urgent priority. To address this, we investigated rumor propagation mechanisms and developed a method to quantify a rumor's influence based on the velocity of new adopters, utilizing search frequency as the primary metric. By analyzing this search frequency, which follows an exponential distribution, we calculated both peak and attenuation coefficients. These coefficients were then treated as target labels for several engineered rumor features. In a 5-fold cross-validation experiment employing mean square error (MSE) as the loss function, decision trees proved optimal for predicting the peak coefficient, while linear regression was ideal for the attenuation coefficient. Feature analysis revealed that precursor attributes were most critical for predicting the outbreak coefficient, whereas location and entity information were paramount for the attenuation coefficient. Furthermore, features that accelerate the initial outbreak often hinder sustained spread, and anxiety was identified as a key driver of rumor generation. Finally, we explored how deep learning techniques, specifically the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model, can be leveraged to minimize forecast errors. This study offers practical, data-driven insights and references for emergency response strategies during the COVID-19 crisis. However, these findings are also applicable to any scenario involving rumor propagation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/andrew008/COVID-19_Rumors.

Achieving accurate distance estimates requires well-sampled PNLFs, as the count of observable PNe correlates with the galaxy's stellar mass. Consequently, researchers must either employ wide-field surveys or concentrate on the bright central regions of galaxies. This study adopts the latter strategy, conducting a census of PNe in the central areas of Fornax cluster galaxies using VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy on early-type galaxies from the Fornax3D survey. By meticulously separating nebular emission from the stellar continuum, we identified [OIII] 5007 {\AA} sources, excluded unresolved impostors and kinematic outliers, and compiled a catalogue of 1350 unique PNe across 21 early-type galaxies. This catalogue includes source positions, [OIII] 5007 {\AA} line magnitudes, and line-of-sight velocities. Leveraging these catalogued PNe, we derived independent distance estimates for each galaxy by fitting the observed PNLF while rigorously accounting for detection incompleteness. These individual measurements yield an average distance to the Fornax cluster of 19.86 $\pm$ 0.32 Mpc ($\mu_{PNLF}$ = 31.49 $\pm$ 0.04 mag). We compared this result with distances obtained using two complementary methods—supernovae and main-sequence stars from open clusters—and an aggregate approach combining PNLF and CNLF weights, resulting in a mean Fornax distance of 19.84 $\pm$ 0.31 Mpc ($m_{PNLF+CNLF}$ = 31.47 $\pm$ 0.04 mag). The agreement between these independent measurements reinforces the validity of the technique for determining distances to individual galaxies and the overall cluster. To enable future studies, we publicly release the catalogue of identified PNe, derived from the comprehensive spectral data gathered by the MUSE instrument.

Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. Furthermore, it utilizes a thermodynamic framework grounded in the Coleman–Noll procedure and the principle of minimum dissipation potential, which necessitates that the material dissipation rate be non-negative. Using the most efficient first-principles methodology, we applied the modified EPW approach (a variant of density functional theory) to calculate the phonon dispersion curves of undoped and doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ via quasi-harmonic approximation. Our findings indicate that in the undoped state, Bi$_2$Se$_3$ exhibits partial harmonic stability within the zero-temperature range of 0--100 K. However, following electron doping, the material demonstrates full harmonic stability across all phonon frequencies between 0 and 100 K. These results were derived using the non-colinear full-spin DFT method (collective DFT) within the VASP code, employing the HSE06 exchange correlation functional to accurately model electron interactions. This represents the initial investigation into electron-lattice coupling in doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ using first-principles techniques. The study confirms the harmonic stability of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ after electron doping through the application of collective DFT, full-spin DFT, and the HSE06 functional. Furthermore, the reduction in phonon dispersion after doping suggests lower acoustic modes, which can facilitate cooling processes and facilitate phase transitions. These insights were gathered using state-of-the-art first-principles methods. Finally, the observed decrease in phonon frequency after doping is linked to enhanced electron-phonon coupling, offering a possible explanation for the emergence of superconductivity in Bi$_2$Se$_3$. This superconductivity can be understood as a consequence of the symmetry breaking induced by doping. Keywords: Bi$_2$Se$_3$, Doping, First-principles, Phonon dispersion, Superconductivity, HSE06, VASP, collective DFT, full-spin DFT.

This was originally established by computing noise kernels, which represent the correlators of the stress-energy tensor for quantum fields. This paper revisits the topic using a quantum thermodynamic framework, specifically calculating two key quantities: heat capacity and quantum compressibility for model geometries containing quantum fields at both high and low temperatures. Heat capacity at constant volume serves as a measure of energy density fluctuations relative to the mean; when this ratio reaches or exceeds one, the applicability of the canonical distribution becomes doubtful. Similarly, compressibility at constant pressure acts as a test for the validity of the grand canonical ensemble. We derive the free energy density to obtain expressions for these thermodynamic quantities for thermal and quantum fields across various spacetimes, including 2D Casimir space, the 2D Einstein cylinder, and the 4D ($S^1 \times S^3$) Einstein universe. To explore dimensional dependence, we also derived these quantities for Einstein universes with even spatial dimensions ($S^1 \times S^2$ and $S^1 \times S^4$). This collection of spacetimes allows us to assess the thermodynamic stability of quantum matter fields and draw qualitative conclusions regarding the compatibility conditions necessary for the coexistence of quantum fields and spacetimes, a central challenge in applying thermodynamics to black hole physics and spacetimes with a cosmological constant. Our results align with previous findings by Collins, Fulling, Lee, Mariani, Mottola, Parentani, Percival, Percival, Verlinde, Wald, Wang, Wu, and Zermeno. However, unlike the thermodynamic analysis of black holes, which is constrained by the lack of global equilibrium and spatial homogeneity, this study is not limited by such factors. Consequently, we can identify ranges of parameters—such as temperature, chemical potential (linked to temperature), and spacetime curvature (analogous to pressure)—where neither the canonical nor grand canonical ensembles are viable. The thermodynamic behavior of quantum fields in (1+3)-dimensional Einstein universes reveals a complex dependence on temperature and chemical potential across different spatial dimensions. Specifically, at zero temperature and potential, fields with both periodic and antiperiodic boundary conditions are thermodynamically stable. However, introducing a chemical potential at finite temperature can destabilize the field, necessitating a below-threshold value to restore thermodynamic stability

commonsense reasoning structured as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). In this framework, nodes represent basic concepts, and directed edges denote "leads to" relationships that capture both physical laws (e.g., causality) and pragmatic inferences (e.g., abduction). This structure enables the derivation of sequential inferences through a breadth-first search approach. The DAG is constructed bottom-up using a formal specification language called ATOMIC-MACHINA, which defines complex nodes via simpler ones (physical causality) or inferred nodes (pragmatic abduction). Notably, the system incorporates the Gricean maxims of quantity and manner to refine its representational model. To ensure robustness and generalization, we established a vast corpus of over 10 million commonsense inferences derived from atomic inferences. We demonstrate the utility of ATOMIC and its corpus for training/finetuning Large Language Models (LLMs) to acquire commonsense reasoning capabilities, as well as for teaching/Vectors models the same. Additionally, our results indicate that these models can generalize to new domains and combine learned concepts to perform higher-order reasoning. The entire construction process is automated and scalable; for instance, we successfully built a similar atlas for animal commonsense within a week using our pipeline. The ATOMIC project is fully open-source, comprising three core components: (1) the atlas itself, (2) the construction tool, and (3) the inference corpus. We envision that researchers can leverage this resource to train models on specific domains of interest (e.g., animal commonsense) by efficiently adding new nodes and edges to the existing atlas. Furthermore, prior to any addition process, analyzing the "leads to" connections between a new node and the atlas can yield insightful discoveries regarding the fundamental structures of physical and pragmatic worlds. Finally, the project welcomes contributions from anyone interested in building their own domain-specific atlas. The source code is available at: https://github.com/atomic-project/atomic.

Although the mean-variance optimization problem can be formulated as a system of linear equations using Lagrange multipliers—potentially enabling the exponential speedup of the HHL quantum algorithm—many components of HHL are incompatible with current Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. This paper presents NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid adaptation of HHL designed for end-to-end execution of small-scale portfolio optimization on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL builds upon existing hybrid HHL variants by leveraging new hardware capabilities, including mid-circuit measurement, qubit reset and reuse, and Quantum Conditional Logic (QCL). To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm to implement a QCL-enhanced Phase Estimation on real trapped-ion hardware, specifically the Quantinuum System Model H1-1. Furthermore, the work introduces a novel technique for determining the optimal evolution time for Hamiltonian simulation. Although the primary focus is on portfolio optimization, the proposed methods for scaling HHL are broadly applicable to any problem solvable via HHL within the NISQ era. Empirical results demonstrate that NISQ-HHL offers significant advantages over the total-variational algorithm HESSIAN for problems of this size, exhibiting higher success probability, greater robustness to noise, and superior efficiency in terms of circuit depth. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive guide for readers interested in replicating the study or applying NISQ-HHL to similar challenges.

We demonstrate that the initial $k_n$ values of $\pi_n$, specifically $\pi_n(1),\dots,\pi_n(k_n)$, become asymptotically independent and identically distributed and uniformly distributed over $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ under specific conditions: total variation distance when $k_n = o(\sqrt{n})$ and Kolmogorov distance when $k_n=o(n)$. Random parking offers an engaging method for teaching probability, combinatorics, and statistics. Since its introduction by Pippenger and Valiant in 1979, it has been a prevalent subject at the Summer Park City Mathematics Institute. While most research focuses on characterizing parking functions through various metrics, this work aims to analyze random parking place statistics within the "critical regime." We derive the asymptotic behavior of these statistics using conditioned random walks and establish precise limit theorems for specific cases. Our main finding indicates that a random parking place is uniformly distributed for large distances from the start of the list, except in rare events defined by conditioned random walks. This paper is an expansion of our 2021 Summer PhD thesis from University Paris-Saclay, which can be accessed here.

We report experimental data from NbN nanowires that not only exhibit this critical voltage but also demonstrate its tunability via a side-gate electrode, which induces periodic variations in the critical voltage. Although these findings align qualitatively with predictions regarding quantum interference among coherent phase slip components, the observed tuning period exceeds simple capacitance-based estimates by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, measurements on a single nanowire revealed two distinct, abrupt shifts in this periodicity, providing constraints for detailed theoretical models. We also evaluate the viability of an explanation attributing this behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowire. Ultimately, the unique combination of material, geometry, and operating conditions in our device likely facilitates this unusual physics; consequently, we propose mechanisms for generating similar effects in other systems and outline potential experimental validations. Our results open avenues for utilizing this physics in sensitive nanoscale probes of superconducting nanowires or qubits, as well as in precise determinations of fundamental constants.

In this study, we experimentally demonstrate using femtosecond laser writing that fundamental and excited orbital states can couple when situated at distinct spatial locations. We provide a comprehensive characterization of an asymmetric double-well-like potential and employ a scanning method to effectively map dynamics along the propagation axis. This key observation directly addresses the need for a spatial mode converter device, which can be integrated anywhere within a photonic glass chip. Leveraging the phase structure of higher-order photonic modes and the effective negative coupling generated, we propose a trimer configuration functioning as a phase beam splitter ($\pi$-BS), offering significant potential for multiplexing and interference-based photonic concatenated operations. Our findings experimentally validate a $\pi$-BS with a measured phase difference of $2.15\pm 0.05$ radians (corresponding to $\pi-0.11$), which exceeds the theoretical prediction of $\pi/2$, along with a phase shifter implementation. These results highlight the practical utility of interferometric schemes relying on internal coupling constants, such as excited orbital states, for precise phase shift measurements and their application in multiplexing protocols. Furthermore, these mechanisms can be harnessed to realize topological photonic systems, including those exhibiting robust edge states at interfaces between materials with opposite effective negative couplings, or to create complex photonic molecules and enhance non-linear effects at positions distinct from the excitation source. This capability to interconnect any two points via excited orbital states provides a crucial tool for the targeted assembly of functional photonic structures within photonic glass chips.

This study investigates airborne infection risks on an urban bus by employing unsteady Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes equations alongside a passive-scalar model for virus-laden aerosol concentrations. The simulation outcomes are contrasted with the commonly used well-mixed model, revealing marked discrepancies in both the concentration distribution and the count of inhaled particles. Specifically, under conditions of low mechanical ventilation, the well-mixed model tends to overestimate concentrations away from the infected passenger while significantly underestimating them in close proximity. These findings are also relevant to other enclosed environments. To better understand the flow and contamination patterns, various airflow scenarios were simulated, including conditions of no masking and mask usage, as well as mechanical and passive ventilation configurations. These results are visualized through contour plots, velocity vectors, and particle concentration histograms, and they align with available experimental data. The study concludes by offering recommendations for optimizing mechanical ventilation and masking strategies to lower infection probabilities, based on the simulated concentration profiles and airflow behaviors.

This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, including graphene and ferromagnetic layers. Manipulating spin-orbit coupling offers a potential route to uncover novel and exotic phases within superconducting and semimetallic systems. In this study, we investigate the magnetoelectrical transport properties—specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect—in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers to identify signatures of the spin-orbit proximity effect and determine its origin. Our findings suggest an increase in the spontaneous magnetic anisotropy of both resistivity and anomalous Hall resistivity at very low Cobalt thicknesses. Furthermore, the analysis of anomalous Hall resistivity indicates that the Bismuth layers alter the Hall effect scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, implying that the spin-orbit proximity effect may arise from the elastic scattering of Cobalt free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. Additionally, the variation in magnetoresistance is attributed to the spin-dependent scattering of carriers at both interfaces and bulk regions. These results provide insights into the fundamental scattering mechanisms at the interface between dissimilar metals, which are crucial for the design of spintronic devices.

Lowering the radiotracer dose or scan duration to mitigate this risk reduces photon counts, thereby compromising image quality. While recent deep neural network (DNN) techniques can translate low-quality PET images—acquired with significantly reduced doses—into high-quality results by leveraging corresponding MRI data, these methods often struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differs statistically from their training sets. We introduce a novel DNN approach that incorporates (i) the fundamental sinogram physics of PET imaging and (ii) uncertainty quantification via per-voxel heteroscedasticity in the residuals between predicted and reference images. This proposed framework, termed suDNN, generates standard-dose PET images from multimodal inputs consisting of low-dose/low-count PET and multi-contrast MRI data, enhancing its robustness against OOD acquisitions. Empirical results on in vivo PET-MRI data and various OOD scenarios demonstrate that suDNN outperforms current state-of-the-art methods both quantitatively and qualitatively. Furthermore, uncertainty assessments align with expected outcomes, correctly identifying regions with high OOD likelihood, such as anatomical areas absent in training data (e.g., the bladder) or organs missing in MRI sequences (e.g., the lungs). By integrating physical principles and uncertainty modeling, our approach offers a superior solution for PET-MRI image reconstruction. This study explores the relationship between Centering Theory and contemporary coreference resolution systems. We propose an operational definition of centering and employ a search-based methodology to systematically evaluate whether neural coreference resolvers comply with CT rules through various discourse metrics. Our information-theoretic analysis indicates a positive correlation between coreference and centering, yet demonstrates that high-performing neural resolvers gain little advantage from explicitly modeling centering concepts. Furthermore, we find that contextualized embeddings encapsulate much of the necessary coherence information, explaining why CT yields minimal improvements for modern neural systems utilizing pretrained representations. Finally, we address coreference factors unmodeled by standard CT, such as world knowledge and recency bias. By formulating an enhanced version of CT that incorporates recency, we show it captures coreference information more effectively than the original formulation. These findings suggest that coreference is encoded in linguistic patterns rather than purely discourse-level representations like centering, and that contemporary systems implicitly model many of these patterns. Consequently, we recommend evaluating coreference resolvers using standardized datasets with coherent annotations and assessing performance solely on structural aspects not already captured by embeddings. Coreference resolution remains a challenging NLP task because coreferent expressions for a specific entity are distributed throughout an argument and influenced by numerous factors beyond context window limits. While numerous enhancements can marginally improve performance, no single modification has proven universally effective. This paper investigates if centering theory—a standard for discourse structure analysis—can be leveraged to enhance coreference resolution. Our results reveal that while texts inherently contain coreference information, state-of-the-art systems implicitly model much of it, making it difficult to isolate centering as a distinct factor. We detail several potential sources of confusion when attempting to evaluate the impact of centering on coreference resolution. Although centering theory does not account for all coreference phenomena (e.g., world knowledge), extending the theory to include recency as a proximity measure better encapsulates this coreference information. This suggests that coreference is primarily determined by language intrinsic to contextual embeddings, with discourse structure playing a secondary role. Consequently, we advise against optimizing models for specific centering properties during coreference resolution; instead, researchers should utilize naturally coherent datasets and evaluate performance only on aspects not already modeled by contextual representations.

WiFi fingerprinting, which involves gathering Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) measurements at known locations, is a prevalent technique in various positioning algorithms found in existing literature. However, accurately calculating the spatial distance between fingerprints is highly dependent on the choice of signal distance function used to map RSSI values to space. This study proposes the use of the 1D Gaussian kernel density estimator (KDE) to determine spatial distances between nodes. To validate this approach, we compare our proposed method against established signal distance metrics using a standard 2D localization dataset collected in an office setting. Additionally, we introduce a novel signal distance function derived from a 2D Gaussian kernel density map, evaluating its performance using the same test dataset. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed 2D-Gaussian KDE significantly enhances the accuracy of popular location estimation methods, including nearest neighbor (NN), weighted NN, location angular distribution (LAD), and fingerprint classification (FC). Specifically, our approach yields a 50% improvement in NN, a 35% gain in weighted NN, a 25% boost in LAD, and a 20% increase in FC accuracy compared to raw RSSI data. These results confirm that treating WiFi signals as probabilistic data via 1D and 2D-Gaussian KDEs offers superior location estimation performance. The source code for our dataset and algorithm is accessible at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/346410440_1D_and_2D-Gaussian_KDE_for_Indoor_Localization.
