K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. First, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the conformal embeddability of spaces with a betweenness relation into Euclidean spaces, noting that this condition implies the metric constraint introduced by J. Mappus. We further demonstrate that our condition subsumes J. Mappus's results in three-dimensional space and produce a corresponding necessary condition for conformal embeddability into Hilbert spaces. Additionally, we examine the conformal embeddability of spaces defined by the axioms of Hilbert geometry into Euclidean spaces. Second, we revisited the question of when a specific class of Hilbert spaces admits an isometric mapping into Euclidean space that preserves the angle function between triples; we provided multiple representations of the image of this mapping and derived its necessary conditions. These findings extend previous work by N. Sierdzsinska-Pa\'zewska and E. \v{S}ev\v{c}ek. Finally, we address the scenario where the range of the angle function is restricted to $(0,\pi)$. To structure the article, we begin with the introduction of betweenness relation-based spaces and a revised definition of the angle function, followed by essential lemmas and their proofs. We conclude with references.

For a number field $K$ of degree $n$ with embeddings $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$ into $\mathbb{C}$, the norm is defined as $\lvert x \rvert = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\lvert \sigma_i(x)\rvert^2}$ for any $x \in K$. Under this norm, an order $\mathcal{O}$ in such a field possesses successive minima satisfying $1=\lambda_0 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$. Inspired by a conjecture of Lenstra, our objective is to identify which inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, where $f_1, \dots, f_{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}$, are valid for an infinite collection $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders in degree $n$ fields. In numerous scenarios—including when $\mathcal{S}$ comprises all isomorphism classes of orders in degree $n$ fields or those with fixed subfield degrees—we establish a full classification of the inequalities $\lambda_k \ll \lambda_i\lambda_j$. Furthermore, we derive analogous results for the quantities $\log \lambda_k$. As a consequence, we obtain a precise criterion for an infinite set of isomorphism classes of orders in degree $n$ fields to possess supersingular places of degree $d$. Our findings generalize several recent discoveries by Breuer, Robert, and Zauderchuk. Additionally, we apply these results to address a specific problem raised by Brumer and Lemmermeyer regarding principal ideals within quadratic orders. An appendix by Brumer elaborates on the arithmetic implications of our main theorems.

Although these schemes have operated for more than a hundred years, their internal dynamics and community structures have remained unstudied due to the opaque nature of participant transactions. This paper offers an empirical investigation of Forsage, a pyramid scheme executed via a smart contract that became one of Ethereum's most resource-intensive applications at its peak. Pyramid schemes have remained a prominent news topic for over a century, yet their execution through smart contracts has remained unexplored until now. These schemes function by prompting users to purchase coins or assets at a current price that is repeatedly halved throughout a fixed periods-based protocol, creating a multi-tiered hierarchy. As long as new users continue to join, the scheme expands; however, once recruitment slows, older tiers are unable to be paid in full, leading to a crash. This study presents an empirical analysis of the pyramid scheme on the Ethereum network inspired by the "Ethereum Classic" game on the Forsage website. By utilizing a heuristic algorithm, we identified the primary profit extraction protocols that allowed key figures to earn multi-million-dollar profits. Our results indicate that external factors, such as coverage by mainstream media, were as critical in causing the scheme's collapse as the inherent limited expansion capacity of pyramid structures. Furthermore, our analysis of the schemes' protocols and profit distributions may aid in the future detection of similar activities. We operate within the full information model, wherein Byzantine nodes possess complete awareness of the network's state at every step—including all random choices—unlimited computational capabilities, and the freedom to deviate arbitrarily from the protocol. Our primary contribution is a randomized distributed algorithm capable of estimating network size despite a high volume of Byzantine nodes. Specifically, this algorithm accurately estimates the size of sparse, small-world expander networks containing up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ Byzantine nodes, where $n$ represents the unknown network size and $\delta$ is any fixed positive constant. The algorithm produces a constant-factor estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability, ensuring that a large majority ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction) of honest nodes obtain the correct network size. Furthermore, the approach is fully distributed, lightweight, and easy to implement; it completes in $O(\log^3{n})$ rounds, utilizes small messages per round, and imposes minimal local computational costs on each node. It is important to note that achieving accurate network size estimation in a sparse network is inherently difficult due to the inability of nodes to explore the entire graph within polynomial time. This hardness is particularly pronounced when Byzantine nodes are present, as they can easily disrupt information gathering in unknown networks. Prior solutions were limited to network sizes polynomial in $n$ and depended heavily on the known value of $\delta$. In contrast, our solution addresses sparse, small-world expanders—whose size grows super-polynomially—and applies to a broader class of unknown networks. The algorithm achieves this by accumulating a precise estimate of $\log(n)$, a task that is fundamentally challenging in such environments. Our approach relies on a new framework involving a "gathering phase" to collect a sufficient number of samples from the network, followed by a "counting phase" that accurately determines $n$ from these samples. This solution assumes the full information model. In a related but weaker adaptive bounded randomness model, authors from ITTJ08 and CDD16 achieved similar results using a more complex algorithm with higher overhead. However, our solution is significantly simpler, accurate within a smaller factor (specifically $1/\sqrt{\log{n}}$), and effective for any small $\delta$, including zero. The network topology is formally defined as a small-world expanders graph, a class of sparse graphs that encompasses random graphs and many naturally occurring networks. management. This research proposes a combinatorial, nonparametric method to estimate short-term queue lengths on a cycle-by-cycle basis using partially observed data from probe vehicles. Unlike traditional approaches, this method avoids assumptions about random arrivals and eliminates the need for primary parameters or complex estimations, relying instead on straightforward algebraic formulas based solely on signal timing. Specifically, for approach lanes at intersections, conditional queue lengths—given probe vehicle location, count, time, and analysis interval (such as the end of a red phase)—are modeled using a Negative Hypergeometric distribution. When validated against field test data involving probe vehicles, the resulting estimators demonstrate accuracy comparable to both parametric methods and standard Highway Capacity Manual procedures. However, these improvements are most significant during partial red phases before vehicles begin to clear the approach lane. Overall, the method requires no calibration; its cycle-by-cycle calculations utilize fully observable data, such as signal timing and probe vehicle attributes (location and time), making it readily applicable in practical traffic management settings. The ultimate goal is to replace potentially inaccurate assumptions regarding queue discharge rates found in current real-time traffic models with this calibration-free estimator. Furthermore, because the approach lane's length is determined by the combination of probe vehicle position and count, this technique can also estimate these metrics for through lanes on freeways by leveraging the same nonparametric, calibration-free framework.

We propose a novel approach rooted in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Unlike conventional methods that treat the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation for a specified mean curvature $K$, our method solves an algebraic equation for $K$ given a chosen conformal factor. This strategy circumvents the challenges regarding the existence and uniqueness of Hamiltonian constraint solutions without resorting to the standard rescaling of source terms, a feature that is critical when sources are fundamental fields, as reconstructing their configurations from rescaled data can be problematic. Employing an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this technique yields rapidly convergent solutions for several previously unexplored initial conditions in numerical relativity: specifically, (i) periodic inhomogeneous spacetimes featuring large random Gaussian scalar field perturbations, and (ii) asymptotically flat black hole spacetimes containing rotating scalar clouds. Validation against analytical solutions and comparisons with existing literature confirm the effectiveness of this new constraint satisfaction method. The code implementing this procedure is publicly accessible at https://github.com/AlexandrePierobon/My CCTD Code. The algorithm can be readily adapted to incorporate momentum constraints and is applicable to any problem where CTT is utilized, including Gravitational Wave generation. We anticipate this code will prove useful to the broader computational relativity community.

Antiferromagnetic antiperovskites represent an emerging class of materials that display diverse properties driven by their intricate electronic band structures and magnetic ordering. However, reports on the anomalous Nernst effect and its magnitude within this specific class remain scarce, a limitation likely attributed to the experimental challenges in accurately determining the anomalous Nernst coefficient. In this study, we present experiments on the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN antiferromagnetic antiperovskite thin films. By utilizing the same sample and measurement geometry for both the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects, we enable a direct comparison between these phenomena to precisely quantify the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. Furthermore, we rigorously assess the spatial distribution of the thermal gradient across the sample and employ finite element modeling to validate our experimental findings. While the local analyses of both effects reveal similar spatial profiles, we demonstrate through finite element simulations that our standard measurement technique significantly underestimates the anomalous Nernst voltage. Our results in Mn$_3$NiN align closely with those from a recent bulk measurement, although the precise value of the anomalous Nernst coefficient remains uncertain due to variations in antiferromagnetic domain structures. We also examine the temperature-dependent behavior of the anomalous Nernst coefficient, again accounting for thermal gradients induced by the current and the sample's geometry through finite element analysis. Ultimately, we establish a quantitative framework to evaluate the spatial thermal gradient and explain the temperature-dependent trends observed in our data. Although finite element modeling was specifically crafted for Mn$_3$NiN, it can be readily adapted to analyze similar antiferromagnetic antiperovskites, as these materials often exhibit competing and unique electronic and magnetic orders that warrant further investigation into their thermoelectric properties. Accurately assessing the thermal gradient is not only critical for correctly interpreting experimental data in Mn$_3$NiN and related compounds but also broadly relevant to thermoelectric measurements in other thin-film devices.

iller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex failure modes such as delaminations that are challenging to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable composites to "see" damage with both good accuracy and high resolution. Furthermore, this enhanced capability for damage identification is essential for developing robust self-healing composites, thereby creating advanced materials that are not only safer but also autonomous.

The vast diversity of life has resulted in a wide array of locomotive designs and methods, with various creatures utilizing legs, wings, fins, and other mechanisms to traverse their environments. This report defines the movement of general biological species as biolocomotion and introduces a computational method to identify it within raw video footage. Crucially, the motion of biological entities navigating an environment can be modeled as a superposition of overall positional advancement and an asymmetric oscillatory pattern; this signature is notably absent in non-biological objects in motion. By leveraging this characteristic signature alongside the distinction between an object's global movement (extrinsic motion) and the localized movement of its parts (intrinsic motion), we developed an algorithm to measure these traits in tracked objects to determine if they represent a biological entity in locomotion. Additionally, an alternative algorithm based on generic features and machine learning, assembled from related research areas, is presented for comparative analysis. The study provides a novel dataset of biolocomotion featuring a broad spectrum of biological and non-biological objects in natural settings, along with annotations for an existing camouflage animal dataset. Quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the alternative approach, validating the hypothesis that biolocomotion can be reliably detected through its unique signature of positional advance with asymmetric oscillation and the disparity between extrinsic and intrinsic motion. Furthermore, the research confirms that machine learning models can effectively learn from related features to identify animals in motion without explicit training on biolocomotion signatures. Finally, the work underscores the ecological significance of detecting biolocomotion for applications such as animal foraging, habitat discovery, and the study of camouflage and counter-camouflage strategies. Recent advances in the algorithms, dataset, and related research are highlighted, offering a foundation for future investigations into animal behavior, such as foraging patterns, habitat selection, and the evolutionary dynamics of camouflage and counter-camouflage.

Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Comprehensive numerical experiments are conducted to validate these theoretical findings and compare NN against other iterative algorithms, including lower-order methods like NS, NI, and CI, as well as high-order alternatives such as Householder and Schur-Faddeev. The results indicate that NN is particularly effective for invertible matrices of sizes 100x100, 500x500, and 1000x1000. Finally, we apply the NN method to estimate Hermitian matrix inverses and solve corresponding linear systems, yielding satisfactory outcomes. Regarding sparse matrices, we present two solutions for可invertible positive sparse matrices and two additional solutions for asymmetric sparse matrices within the main text. Across all scenarios, we establish an analytical expression for the total computational cost of NN, which aligns with empirical observations. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that NN is a highly promising algorithm for calculating matrix inverses and solving linear systems.

In this study, we investigate the topological and localization characteristics of a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model featuring spatially correlated random binary disorder. Our findings reveal that such binary disorder can trigger a transition from a trivial insulator to a topological Anderson insulator across multiple parameter regimes. These topological Anderson insulators are identified by a disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states, observable via the inverse participation ratio in both real and momentum spaces. Because the time step necessary to resolve collision dynamics is significantly smaller than that required for fluid flow, the computational expense of using the traditional soft-sphere model—which mandates such small steps—becomes prohibitive for simulations involving thousands of particles. While existing state-of-the-art methods artificially stretch the collision time to match several flow solver time steps, this approach introduces non-physical artifacts that compromise simulation results. In contrast, the proposed MTSA employs distinct time steps to independently resolve fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. The algorithm was evaluated against both particle-wall and particle-particle collisions, with optimal substep iterations determined to achieve excellent alignment between experimental data and results from the traditional soft-sphere model. Subsequently, the MTSA was applied to a sediment transport simulation (turbulent flow over an erodible bed) involving thousands of particles. Comparisons with the collision time stretching method revealed that the latter reduces particle stiffness, diminishes particle entrainment, and distorts turbulence and particle statistics. Ultimately, the MTSA achieved a computational cost reduction of approximately one order of magnitude compared to the traditional soft-sphere model while maintaining nearly identical accuracy. This significant decrease in computational expense is expected to encourage the widespread adoption of particle-resolved simulations in future research. Iterative substep calculations can be implemented in parallel; therefore, further minimizing the substep time step size is unlikely to lower overall computational expenses.

Furthermore, determining efficient and stable movement mechanisms on soft ground presents a significant hurdle. This study aims to control a one-dimensional monopod hopper to achieve a target jump height. To accomplish this, I first established and validated a discrete element method (DEM) simulation environment featuring spherical granular material as the soft ground. Using this setup, I developed ground reaction force models based on resistive force theory (RFT). These RFT models were then employed to create a feedforward force control system for the robot. Within the DEM simulation, a feedback control loop was implemented to correct deviations between the actual ground reaction forces and the RFT predictions. Consequently, the robot successfully tracked desired trajectories and reached the target height within five hops, significantly reducing apex position errors compared to using feedforward control alone. Additionally, the experiment varied the robot's square foot area from 1cm² to 49cm². The results demonstrate that the feedback controller effectively manages fluctuations in ground reaction forces, even when the foot dimensions are comparable to the size of individual grains. However, when the foot area exceeded 25cm², the apex position error surpassed 10cm, indicating that excessive increase in foot area is counterproductive for hopping over granular media. This outcome aligns with the observed decline in the coefficient of restitution at low impact velocities as foot area grows. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first report highlighting the adverse effects of enlarging feet on a monopod hopper's performance when locomoting on granular grounds. The findings offer valuable insights for future designs of legged robots intended to operate on soft terrains.

Elastically scattered mesons can be elastically scattered off protons, nuclei, or other mesons; for instance, the CLAS12 experiment at Jefferson Lab in USA, the EIC, and the FCC are specifically designed to measure the charge radii of scalar, pseudoscalar, vector, and axial-vector mesons with high precision. This information is crucial for validating the contact interaction model and its predictions regarding elastic form factors, particularly in light of the upcoming high-precision data from the EIC and FCC. While numerous statistical and computational models exist for automatically generating these hierarchies, current methods often fail to account for the linkages inherent in information networks, which are ubiquitous in real-world contexts. Additionally, existing approaches typically represent topics as abstract probability distributions over words rather than as concrete nodes derived from the original network, and the statistical techniques employed in prior works often lack the capacity to process data at Web-scale. This paper introduces the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), which leverages a distributed vertex-programming process to compute a nonparametric Bayesian generative model. Experimental results on three medium-sized datasets and the complete Wikipedia dataset demonstrate that HDTM is capable of inferring accurate hierarchies even when applied to large-scale information networks. Comparative analyses against state-of-the-art algorithms reveal that HDTM produces more accurate and higher-quality hierarchies by simultaneously modeling both the structural relationships and content of web documents. Furthermore, the study confirms that modern computing platforms can process billions of web-scale documents within hours using this programming approach. The HDTM represents a substantial advancement over previous methods, offering a robust solution for deriving meaningful and scalable hierarchies from information networks. Performance gains were particularly evident on Wikipedia, likely due to its rich internal linking structure. To illustrate the potential applications of this work, the paper highlights two primary uses: (1) enabling efficient roaming through human-navigable information spaces, and (2) facilitating the integration of new documents into established hierarchies.

Annealing involves slowly varying Hamiltonian parameters to explore equilibrium phases, making it a powerful method for solving complex optimization tasks. Conversely, quenches entail sudden Hamiltonian changes that drive the system into a non-equilibrium state. This study examines the connection between these two approaches, demonstrating that the critical bottleneck of quantum annealing—the minimum of the annealing gap—can be identified through a dynamical quench parameter characterizing the post-quench quantum state. By integrating statistical methods, such as neural network training, with quench data, we can reconstruct the complete functional behavior of the annealing gap. We further show that insights gained regarding the annealing gap, either partially or fully, enable the design of optimized quantum annealing protocols, yielding practical improvements in time-to-solution. These findings are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians, which model challenging instances of the exact cover problem. Our results indicate that, with access to partial quench information, one can achieve a safe factor-of-two increase in annealing time for specific problems on current superconducting devices without compromising success probability. More broadly, our approach offers a systematic framework for diagnosing quench dynamics and integrating this data to enhance the performance of quantum annealers.

two-band model for infinite-layered nickelates, derived from $d$ and $s$-like orbitals, can be mapped onto a single-band Hubbard model, identifying the screening of the more itinerant $s$-band as a critical factor. Without screening, a strongly correlated band yields an antiferromagnetic ground state. Under weak screening, strong correlations drive electrons out of the $s$-band, resulting in an undoped Mott insulator with half-filled $d$ orbitals; this scenario contrasts with high-$T_c$ cuprate observations and suggests $s$-wave pairing for the superconducting state. Conversely, strong screening leads to partially filled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands that couple weakly, resembling a self-doped $d$ band with tendencies toward $d$-wave pairing. Specifically, in the strong screening regime, mapping to a one-band model reveals interesting spectral weight transfers when a second $s$ band is self-doped. Consequently, we conclude that both one-band physics and a Kondo-lattice-like regime arise from the same two-orbital model, contingent upon the strength of electronic correlations and the screening of the $s$-band. These findings indicate that two-band models can replicate the experimental properties of infinite-layer nickelates, particularly the currently observed $d$-wave-like superconductivity, while also accounting for $s$-wave symmetry in thinner, experimentally realizable structures. Finally, we discuss the challenges associated with actually achieving this configuration. Throughout our analysis, all conclusions are drawn by comparing spectral functions and correlation functions, with the latter serving as robust indicators of the system's ground state symmetry. Our approach avoids relying on Hamiltonian coefficients that lack clear physical meaning within an $LDA+U$ framework, thereby circumventing the well-documented difficulties in determining relevant parameters for nickelates.

Suitable squeezing and displacement parameters are determined such that the state fidelity relative to a metrologically sensitive compass state exceeds 99%. Furthermore, the variance in measurements of small shifts is found to be identical for both the proposed states and the compass states, exhibiting comparable behavior as the average photon number changes. In terms of metrological applications, the low number variance of the compass state at low coherent amplitudes indicates its potential for estimating the damping parameter. Additionally, the variance of the real part of the state at negative imaginary values demonstrates its utility in estimating the damping factor. The small number variance at high imaginary values facilitates the estimation of the phase parameter, and the variance of the imaginary component underscores the state's effectiveness in measuring the anharmonicity parameter. Finally, the low number variance observed in the origin across all cases highlights the state's potential for determining the analysis angle. As a metrological tool, the small photon number variance of our SQDS states enables efficient and simultaneous estimation of pairs of parameters, such as (damping, phase) or (anharmonicity, analysis angle). The varying behavior of uncertainty in the (damping, phase) pair confirms the state's suitability for Heisenberg-limited sensing, a property not seen in the squeezed number state (SSN). In the (anharmonicity, analysis angle) pair, the uncertainty in the analysis angle follows a 1/N law, whereas the Cram\'er-Rao bound approximates the uncertainty in anharmonicity for small values of |$\alpha$| and $\squeezing$. The primary advantage of this new state lies in its low number variance at the origin, a feature shared by displaced number states (DSN), which allows for efficient and simultaneous parameter estimation. This variance also proves critical in Heisenberg-limited sensing for the (damping, phase) pair. Overall, the low number variance at the origin makes this state highly promising for metrological sensing and measurement across multiple parameters. Compared to existing states like displaced number, squeezed number, and even the metrologically sensitive compass state, our proposed SQDS state requires lower energy to estimate the same set of parameters, making it a superior choice for heuristic small-parameter estimation and metrological sensing. The unique characteristics of this state in characterizing dark states (DPB) expand its potential to become a significant heuristic for estimating magnetic field parameters.

While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm eliminates the VSI zone entirely. We also examined the impact of an external photoevaporative wind, which was shown to suppress cooling and elicit the VSI before dust evolution could stabilize it. These findings suggest that efficient dust settling in the outer disks may hinder VSI-driven dust accumulation. Furthermore, this mechanism offers a means to drive VSI photoevaporation in the outer disk, a process that can be inhibited by dust growth, thereby creating a photoevaporative scenario distinct from the traditional outside-in evaporation pattern. Finally, we note that this external photoevaporation can expose polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) to the interstellar radiation field, potentially accounting for the recently observed PAH signal in the disk around V4048.

These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of the training data to be poisoned. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks are now feasible with a few-shot data poisoning approach. Furthermore, we show that this attack method can infiltrate classification models designed to adhere to privacy constraints, such as those trained via federated learning. Unlike previous attempts, our approach minimizes data poisoning costs while avoiding static triggers, thereby offering a potent and harder-to-detect threat. We detail the attack mechanism and support our claims with both experimental results and theoretical analysis. Finally, we extend the attack model to apply to text classification. This research carries significant privacy implications, particularly for protecting sensitive data in applications like health monitoring and smart home devices. Consequently, our findings underscore the urgent need for detection methods that can identify such attacks without needing to know the specific location of the backdoor.

light propagation models grounded in the parametrised post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism, a framework designed to test potential deviations from general relativity. Among these effects, the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$, which quantifies gravitational light deflection, significantly influences astrometric data. This study analytically and numerically investigates how deviations of $\gamma$ from its general relativity value of unity impact parallax measurements in Gaia-like systems. Analytical calculations determined the changes in observable quantities resulting from minor variations in PPN $\gamma$, while numerical simulations were conducted to verify how these observable shifts translate into parallax estimation errors. The results indicate that a deviation in $\gamma$ causes a global parallax shift; a corresponding formula for this bias was derived, incorporating the satellite's barycentric distance, the angle between the spin axis and the Sun, and the uncertainty in $\gamma$. Numerical simulations of astrometric solutions corroborate these theoretical findings. Current estimates of PPN $\gamma$ suggest that the contribution to the Gaia parallax zero point is unlikely to exceed 0.2 $\mu$as. Furthermore, simulations reveal a strong dependence of the parallax shift on ecliptic latitude, an effect attributed to an asymmetry in the Gaia scanning law. This conclusion is fully supported by additional simulations utilizing a reversed precession direction for the spin axis relative to the Sun.

answering questions requiring commonsense background is common practice, yet it risks introducing noise and misleading data due to the vastness of available information. To address the challenge of effectively integrating relevant knowledge, we introduce a semantic-driven, knowledge-aware Question Answering framework that regulates knowledge injection through a coarse-to-fine approach. This framework employs a tailoring strategy to filter extracted knowledge based on the coarse semantics of the query during the extraction phase. Additionally, we developed a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that leverages structural knowledge to hierarchically fuse appropriate information according to the fine-grained semantics of the questions. Experimental results on the CommonsenseQA dataset show that our proposed method outperforms strong baseline approaches. Furthermore, a case analysis highlights the positive impact of our coarse-to-fine knowledge injection strategy. The code for our framework is available at: https://github.com/YanlongZhang/KAMQAM.

Large language models (LLMs) have recently been extended with reasoning capabilities through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, which enhances performance on complex tasks by guiding models to generate intermediate reasoning steps. However, in free-generation settings, CoT often produces numerous noisy thoughts that can distract the model from the core answer. To mitigate this noise, various filtering methods have been proposed to extract valuable components from generated texts; however, these approaches remain computationally expensive and still struggle with the high volume of extracted semantic data. This paper introduces a lightweight semantic fusion framework designed to address noise reduction in large-scale chain-of-thought knowledge. By incorporating hierarchical knowledge structure and a progressive fusion strategy, our method hierarchically integrates semantic information and adaptively adjusts the weight of knowledge at different levels within the large-scale CoT generation process. Experimental results across three small-scale natural language understanding datasets and one large-scale legal dataset demonstrate that our approach surpasses strong baseline methods. Additionally, a case analysis confirms the effectiveness of our hierarchical semantic fusion strategy for large-scale chain-of-thought knowledge. Our code is accessible at: https://github.com/YanlongZhang/LargeScaleCoTNoiseReduction.

A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm and provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing random walk methods. Furthermore, we extend this approach to general sampling strategies and algorithms suitable for graph data that is not centrally stored. Source code for our algorithms and benchmarks is available at https://github.com/harshdeshmukh19/RWLearn.

This metric captures the variety of local atomic arrangements as a continuous scale ranging from solid to liquid phases, defined relative to a distribution of thermal fluctuations. The objective is to estimate $E_G(\eta(\theta)) \equiv \eta_G$ using independent observations $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$, given that $Y_i \sim f(y|\theta_i)$ and $\theta_i \sim G$ are independent and identically distributed. This work investigates Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) for this scenario, outlining their fundamental properties and representations. Specifically, we propose a novel viewpoint on the weak convergence result by Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956), extending its implications to a setting where $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_n$ are treated as fixed parameters. Furthermore, we connect the problem of estimating $\eta_G$ to non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation under squared loss. The paper also presents applications of GMLE to sampling issues, demonstrating estimator performance through both simulations and an analysis of real data. Notably, when $\eta(\theta) = \theta$, the GMLE reduces to the empirical Bayes method introduced by Efron and Stein (1999). Generalized maximum likelihood estimation is a potent tool yielding excellent outcomes in various contexts; however, its implementation relies on solving a system of integral equations. To our knowledge, no general-purpose software currently exists to compute GMLE. We introduce an algorithm designed to apply KMLE to scenarios where θ represents the cluster of observations generated by the same random effect. This algorithm extends the approach of Efron and Stein (1999) by producing estimates with markedly superior performance in several tested examples.

While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and rigorous evaluation of these methods remains difficult. First, existing data preprocessing steps are often proprietary and custom-tailored, hindering experimental standardization. Second, current DLKT studies frequently employ inconsistent evaluation protocols that lack alignment with real-world educational settings. To resolve these issues, we present \textsc{pyKT}, a comprehensive Python-based benchmark platform designed to ensure valid comparisons across DLKT methods through exhaustive evaluations. The \textsc{pyKT} library features standardized, integrated preprocessing procedures for seven popular datasets across various domains, along with implementations of ten frequently compared DLKT models to facilitate transparent experimentation. Our rigorous, fine-grained empirical studies reveal key insights for effective DLKT, such as how incorrect evaluation settings can cause label leakage and artificially inflate performance, and how many recent DLKT improvements are marginal compared to the initial model by Piech et al. \cite{piech2015deep}. We have open-sourced both \textsc{pyKT} and our experimental findings at https://pykt.org/, and we invite contributions from other research groups and practitioners. \textsc{pyKT} is also accessible via TensorFlow Hub at https://huggingface.co/pykt.

SMT solver veriT was introduced a decade ago at the inaugural PxTP workshop. Since that time, the format has evolved significantly. veriT proofs are now employed in various applications, and other solvers also produce proofs using this standard. To inform future enhancements, we seek community feedback. In this process, we examine the format's history, outline our pragmatic development strategy, and address potential issues that may emerge when other solvers utilize the format. Finally, we invite community members to provide their own insights into the format's assessment capabilities and potential enhancement opportunities. Our objective is to ultimately establish a stable proof format aligned with the solver's capabilities. Notably, many of these challenges are broadly relevant to any proof generator and solver combination. We plan to publish this analysis as a separate report alongside our work in CASFAP. The proof format will continue to be tested in CASFAP, evaluated by human proof checkers, and refined based on their feedback. We aim to make the format and associated tests publicly available later this year. Proof generators capable of producing this format include veriT (which has superseded its predecessor PR19), CPCP (an experimental solver), and perhaps others.

This work reports on an automatic assessment of proof readability, conducted by our group and potentially expandable with community input. We achieve this by evaluating proofs generated by veriT using a proof checker we developed specifically for this format. The document is structured into seven sections: introduction, background, design considerations, format specification, examples, conclusion, and references. Additional technical details and figures are available in the machine-readable HTML version. The source code is planned to be released under the 3-clause BSD license alongside our CASFAP submission. We welcome feedback on the format from the verification community and other proof generators, such as CVc5, EProVeT, Lean4, ProofGeneral, and YProVe. While we generally adhere to the "keep it simple and stupid" principle, we acknowledge that simplicity is subjective and that adding features often inadvertently introduces complexity. Although we strive for clarity, errors are inevitable, and we appreciate any feedback. Although we cover most aspects comprehensively, some topics were omitted due to space constraints; these will be published separately. Our goal is eventually to reach a stable state where the format requires no further changes. We thank the referees for their constructive comments, which helped improve the paper's quality. We also thank our group members for their encouragement and support.

Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. To streamline this transfer, we introduce the use of an intermediate alphabet—Czech stripped of accents—and demonstrate that this approach is highly effective. This technique also proves beneficial when applied solely to Czech data, resembling a coarse-to-fine training paradigm. Our results show significant reductions in both training time and word error rate (WER). Specifically, the final WER increased by only 2.8% (from 14.1% to 16.9%) when training a Czech model by first training on data processed with abbreviated Czech, compared to training directly on standard Czech. These findings suggest that acoustic language adaptation is more readily achieved than linguistic language adaptation, making intermediate intermediates a powerful tool for ASR. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ameyer01/ASR-Transfer.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems can benefit from multi-task learning, particularly when additional related data is available. In this study, we examine whether a German ASR model trained using English and German data can be effectively transferred to Czech ASR. We compare two training strategies: training directly on Czech data versus an intermediate approach where the German model is adapted to Czech without accents before final fine-tuning. Our experiments indicate that this intermediate method reduces training time and WER by 50% and 1.6% respectively, compared to baseline direct training. We further analyze the impact of different learning rates and batch sizes for each task within this multi-task framework. Additionally, we investigate the separate effects of unidirectional transfer (English to Czech) and language mixing (training data concatenated) compared to the bidirectional setup. Our results confirm that acoustic transfer is easier to achieve than linguistic transfer, validating the use of intermediate models even for languages that are not highly mutually intelligible. Our experiments with intermediate models and learning rate configurations offer insights into applying multi-task learning to ASR. Like prior work, we employ phonetic embeddings to enhance ASR performance through multi-task learning. However, unlike previous studies, we do not train these embeddings jointly; instead, we use a pre-trained Czech phonetic embedding map. We conclude by discussing how this approach can be extended to other

Marine exploration presents significant challenges for robot navigation, primarily due to time-consuming and noise-prone sonar data used for map building. This paper describes how to integrate a noise-robust grid-based sonar map construction algorithm with an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to enable a underwater robot to localize itself and trace a retrace its path using only front-facing sonar. The algorithm efficiently creates sparse, vectorized map representations from narrow-bandwidth vector sonar beams. These maps are updated via a decision tree classifier, allowing the EKF to predict measurement likelihoods in specific ranges without needing to merge all sonar returns into a single range profile. Simulation and real-world tests using a small, low-cost underwater vehicle demonstrate that this approach yields highly accurate pose estimates from front-facing sonar, even in cluttered scenes with obstacles.

This paper reframes distinct GEC domains as separate tasks and introduces a meta-learning framework for few-shot domain adaptation that requires no pseudo data. In summary, the key contributions are: (a) treating each GEC domain as a unique task to facilitate efficient few-shot domain adaptation, (b) designing an effective meta-learning algorithm for this purpose, and (c) demonstrating the method's efficacy in L1 and L2 GEC domain adaptation scenarios. Experimental evidence validates that this strategy yields significant benefits in data-sparse few-shot domain adaptation cases. We evaluate both approaches on low-resource language pairs, comparing their efficacy against direct training and direct transfer baselines. Our results indicate that direct training and direct transfer yield comparable performance for most pairs. among strategic agents with additive valuations, assuming no monetary transfers. In this context, a mechanism is an algorithm that processes agents' reported valuations rather than their true ones. Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), ultimately providing an affirmative answer. We analyze two algorithms recognized for generating such allocations in non-strategic environments: Round-Robin, which yields EF1 allocations for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method by Plaut and Roughgarden [SIAM Journal of Discrete Mathematics, 2020] that produces EFX allocations for two agents. We demonstrate that all pure Nash equilibria of Round-Robin result in allocations that are EF1 relative to the agents' true values. Furthermore, we show that the Plaut and Roughgarden algorithm not only achieves EFX but also satisfies maximin share fairness in this strategic setting—a property it does not possess in the non-strategic case. Additionally, we prove that a weaker version of this result applies to any two-agent mechanism that consistently yields pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations. We further discuss the limitations of these findings when extended to environments with three or more agents. Our analysis includes detailed examinations of the efficiency of these allocations, measured by both utilitarian and egalitarian welfare, as well as an exploration of how these mechanisms perform in assigning divisible items to strategic agents.

839 exhibits almost no star formation, except for a prominent complex of HII regions situated at the very edge of its outer disc. To investigate the origins and characteristics of this feature, researchers compared new Hα and archival broad-band imaging of UGC 8839 with similar data from four comparable spiral galaxies. The findings suggest that the off-axis star formation in UGC 8839 arises from a hyper-stable, dark matter-dominated disc throughout all radii, where the Toomre parameter reaches its lowest value only in the extreme outer disc. By employing analysis methods specifically tailored to handle the challenges of low surface brightness and small number statistics, the study determined that this HII region complex is not anomalous when modeled with a power-law luminosity function, indicating it is an intrinsic structure rather than a merging satellite. However, the entire population of HII regions in UGC 8839 demonstrates a distinct preference for larger galactocentric distances compared to those in the other sample galaxies. UGC 8839 vividly illustrates the connection between the baryonic-to-dark matter ratio and disc stability. Furthermore, a three-body interaction, resembling a scaled-down version of the mechanism thought to drive star formation in Malin 1, aligns with the observed extreme outer disc activity in UGC 8839's extended disc. A simulation of UGC 8839's three-body system corroborates this configuration and reproduces the observed HII region distribution through enhanced gas accretion triggered by the enhanced disc stability. This study underscores the necessity of advanced analysis techniques for low surface brightness and small number statistics to accurately characterize the extreme outer discs of spiral galaxies. Ultimately, UGC 8839 confirms that the most stable discs can indeed trigger star formation, a phenomenon that can be replicated via increased gas accretion in a three-body system. These mechanisms offer potential explanations for the extended, star-forming discs observed in galaxies such as NGC 1512 and UGC 8839. UGC 8839 serves as a prime example of this process, a model that also accounts for the extreme outer disc activity seen in other large spiral galaxies, including Malin 1, HCG 1, and UGC 9163.

This study examines how our results vary with quark mass and evaluates the significance of correlations between the quark and antiquark inside the pion. Furthermore, we compare our lattice findings with predictions derived from chiral perturbation theory. Ultimately, we formulate precise conditions under which the quark-antiquark correlation in a pion can be considered significant. Lattice QCD offers a controlled environment to query strong interaction dynamics; this work demonstrates how lattice results can be analyzed through an expansion in powers of $1 / QCD scale$. The scenarios and assumptions explored here are directly relevant to interpreting quark-antiquark correlations in spectroscopy, particularly regarding the mechanism of confinement and criteria for hadronization. While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, this is only possible if accretion variability is properly considered. Although variability is significant during the embedded phases of star formation, it is often assumed to be minor in later stages. In this study, we report substantial accretion rate variations observed in the target XX Cha and discuss their implications for population studies of classical T Tauri stars. Comparing mass accretion rates derived from fitting UV-to-near-infrared spectra in recent X-Shooter observations with those measured 11 years prior using the same instrument, we find that XX Cha exhibits nearly 2 dex of accretion variability between 2010 and 2021. While the specific timescales of this variation remain uncertain, XX Cha demonstrates extreme accretion variability for a classical T Tauri star. If such behavior is common among these stars, potentially occurring on timescales longer than previously investigated, it could significantly influence disk evolution models constrained by the observed spread in accretion rates. Finally, we note that earlier studies relying on spectral lines to assess accretion variability may have underestimated the fluctuations in certain active classical T Tauri stars.

However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to mitigate this issue. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network utilizes a differentiable key-value memory mechanism to assign credit to each agent in an offline setting. These decomposed credits facilitate the reconstruction of joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay based on individual trajectories, enabling agents to share high-quality experiences. Subsequently, agents conservatively train their policies using a graph attention network (GAT)-based critic. Evaluations across discrete control environments (StarCraft II and multi-agent particle environments) and continuous control settings (multi-agent MuJoCo) demonstrate that our method yields significantly superior results on complex, mixed offline multi-agent datasets, particularly when there are substantial disparities in the quality of individual trajectories. Source code is available at https://github.com/yzh16999999/SIT-MARL.

Most conventional intensity-based registration techniques rely on optimization algorithms to maximize image similarity; while these often yield satisfactory results for kilovoltage (kV) images, they struggle with MV images due to inferior image quality and typically lack a sufficient capture range. advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. However, these existing approaches require specific adaptations to align with evolving IoV architectures. Meanwhile, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for enhancing data privacy and security within IoVs. Concurrently, Blockchain technology offers significant potential through its secure, decentralized, and auditable mechanisms for data recording and sharing. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the application and implementation of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs. Additionally, it examines potential challenges, proposed solutions, and future research directions associated with these frameworks. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational resource for developing modern Blockchain-Enabled FL solutions to address various data privacy issues and scenarios in IoVs. Concurrently, the authors highlight key research gaps and potential areas of focus for upcoming studies on Blockchain-Enabled FL in IoVs. By employing surveys, the authors utilize appropriate solutions and implementations to effectively integrate FL and Blockchain technologies for data privacy and security, specifically addressing data recording and sharing, encryption and decryption, key management, identity management and authentication, emergency vehicle priority access, and traffic information sharing. Finally, the survey concludes by emphasizing the limitations and limitations of these solutions and implementations.

nova (DN) that experienced a classical nova outburst in 2018, has been monitored via ground-based optical, Swift UV/X-ray, and Fermi-LAT gamma-ray observations for nearly three years post-eruption. Among the fastest-evolving novae observed, V392 Per exhibits a $t_2$ decline time of just 2 days. Early spectral data indicate multiple, interacting mass ejections, with shocks from these events driving both the initial optical brightness and gamma-ray emission. The system entered solar conjunction shortly after the eruption; upon re-emergence, the nova had transitioned into the nebular phase, revealing the tail end of the super-soft X-ray stage. Later optical observations tracked the fading ejecta and a persistent narrow-line emission spectrum originating from the accretion disk. Continued hard X-ray emission suggests a standing accretion shock within an intermediate polar configuration among the main-sequence novae class. By approximately three years after the eruption, the source returned to pre-nova outburst variability. Rapid X-ray transients later rekindled the nova remnant, likely resulting from the collision of remaining ejecta with the accretion disk. Rapid X-ray variability continues to occur infrequently. V392 Per provides an exceptional, well-observed instance of the post-nova recovery process in a system with high mass-transfer rates, characterized by rapid ejection times and an intermediate polar nature. This remnant remains dynamically unstable; future accretion episodes will either eject more matter or sustain transient X-ray variability until equilibrium is reached. Based on measured parameters and assuming an initial K5 main-sequence companion (consistent with post-nova spectral data), the final system comprises a $0.89 \pm 0.04 M_{\odot}$ neutron star and a $0.19 \pm 0.07 M_{\odot}$ white dwarf separated by a $1.6 \pm 0.1 R_{\odot}$ orbit. This configuration ensures recurrent novae or merger timescales of roughly $10^7$ years. Rapid X-ray transients typical of main-sequence novae are anticipated to persist for centuries before the stars merge. Post-nova evolution in such systems can lead to various compact binaries, including magnetic neutron stars or millisecond pulsars.

During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training data and subsequently generates a codebook in an unsupervised fashion by leveraging the model's clustering properties, assigning one codebook entry to each GMM component. In the online phase, the BS offloads the GMM to the mobile terminal (MT) without transferring the codebook; the MT then uses the GMM to identify the most appropriate codebook entry. This process eliminates the need for channel estimation at the MT, as it relies on the observed signal to calculate the responsibility of each GMM component. The feedback transmitted to the BS comprises the index of the component with the highest responsibility, allowing the BS to select the corresponding codebook entry. Simulation results indicate that this proposed design and feedback scheme surpass conventional Lloyd clustering-based algorithms, particularly in scenarios with reduced pilot overhead. Furthermore, the approach is easily adaptable to offline deep learning-based clustering designs by replacing the GMM with other appropriate machine learning models. Furthermore, the proposed scheme supports a distributed codebook update mechanism where mobile terminals participate in GMM data fitting; in this setup, the feedback index serves as a label for data points, enabling a distributed GMM construction where each terminal estimates a specific GMM component. Finally, the core concept of designing a codebook based on GMMs can be broadly applied to other clustering algorithms, as the feedback index corresponds to a data point's class in a standard classifier. We track the dynamical evolution of Pop III compact object binaries as cosmic structures develop, calculating how field stars' dynamical friction drives these remnants into NSCs. Subsequent evolution inside the clusters is modeled through three-body interactions and gravitational-wave (GW) emission. Our results indicate that 7.5% of Pop III binary remnants will migrate to the galactic centers (within 3 pc). Initially, the study focuses on a single-user, single-relay configuration, addressing a joint power optimization problem at the source and relay under individual power constraints for both nodes, with the goal of maximizing the end-to-end secrecy rate through optimal power allocation across sub-carriers. Utilizing a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) approximation for the end-to-end secrecy rate, an optimization problem is defined to jointly optimize power allocation at the base station, relay selection, sub-carrier assignment to users, and power loading at each relay node. Text-based games are a valuable tool for studying how machines and humans acquire common-sense knowledge about actions, objects, and their interactions in physical worlds. Programming benchmarks using these games helps researchers evaluate agents' skills in task execution, world modeling, and reasoning. While recent libraries have sought to standardize this process, their simulation speeds remain unacceptably low, restricting experiments to a maximum of 3,000,000 time steps per day. This bottleneck prevents the large-scale data collection often required for modern AI research, such as day-long experiments involving billion-step counts. We show that current benchmarks can be accelerated significantly using basic techniques and high-performance programming languages like C++. Our method achieves a speedup exceeding 1,000 times over the fastest current implementation (AEGIS) and offers other performance advantages. We release ExpressTextWorld as an open-source library supporting three popular text-based game benchmarks (TextWorld, SCUT, and LC-BQ). We validate the library's effectiveness in standard experiments and demonstrate how simple natural language tasks can be used to train basic agents. ExpressTextWorld is available at https://github.com/amitshukr19/EtextWorld.

a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. We introduce a related yet distinct proposal: the conjecture should instead apply to particles possessing non-negative self-binding energy. This perspective is especially significant in anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, as it admits a straightforward conformal field theory (CFT) dual. Specifically, if $\Delta(q)$ represents the scaling dimension of the lowest-dimension operator carrying charge $q$ under a global $U(1)$ symmetry, then $\Delta(q)$ must be a convex function of $q$. Unlike formulations relying on holographic dual forces or spacetime locality, this approach allows us to boldly conjecture that charge spectrum convexity applies to any unitary CFT, extending beyond those with weakly coupled and weakly curved gravitational duals. We term this the Charge Convexity Conjecture and note its generalization to larger global symmetry groups. Testing this via perturbation theory, $1/N$ expansions, and semi-classical methods in examples where anomalous dimensions are calculable confirms the conjecture in all cases examined. However, the underlying CFT reason for this validity remains unclear. Unlike the case for vacuum vacuum (VV) convexity, which links to entanglement entropy and extremal surfaces, $1/N$ corrections to $\Delta(q)$ exhibit oscillatory behavior that precludes a straightforward generalization involving extremal surfaces. Nevertheless, $\Delta(q)$ remains convex at strong coupling, suggesting an unknown PRD (positive root derivative) property for $\Delta(q)$ in the large $N$ limit that serves as a generalization of extremal surface dynamics. Furthermore, this conjecture connects to spectral density expectations for primary operators decomposed into irreducible representations of the global symmetry group. Ultimately, we relate this framework to the CCWZ embedding tensor of a global symmetry's nonlinear sigma model in AdS$_5$, which encodes the theory's spectrum and interactions; the conjecture corresponds to the positivity of the KK (Kaluza-Klein) mass matrix for bosons. Finally, we briefly extend these ideas to $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills and its S-dual.

By a theorem of D. Goto and K. Nishimura, any Noetherian local ring $R$ admitting a quotient field of prime characteristic $p$ (an $F$-ring) contains a test element. However, no such generalization is known for rings that are not $F$-rings. In this paper, we demonstrate that the quotient field of an excellent local ring serves as a test element. Consequently, we conclude that every $F$-ring possesses a quotient field that acts as a test element. These outcomes extend previous work by J. Craig, H. Chang, and the author. Additionally, the research of T. He, W. Zheng, and Z. Wang is examined.

Yet, current assessments and policy guidance on market design and ancillary services often fail to account for the intricate interactions between markets and services. To address this gap, this paper introduces an open-source agent-based model designed to evaluate design options for electricity markets and ancillary services. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM) integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA toolbox for power system analysis. This model offers adjustable design parameters for both markets and agents, alongside detailed clearing algorithms for day-ahead markets, intra-day continuous trading, redispatch, and imbalances. Additionally, ASAM features extensive policy performance indicators, including new metrics for price mark-ups and redispatch efficiency. A stylized simulation scenario was used to validate the model and explore a specific redispatch design issue. The findings regarding multi-period all-or-none order types in redispatch markets reveal three key implications: (1) The order design minimizes risk for market participants by ensuring full order clearance. (2) Large orders can create dispatch ramps before and after delivery periods, potentially triggering ramp-risk mark-ups and necessitating extra intra-day imbalance trading. (3) In liquid market conditions, an all-or-none design leads to grid operator over-procurement of redispatch because partial order activation is impossible; furthermore, incomplete activation often forces grid operators to introduce system imbalances, as upward and downward redispatch volumes become unequal. These results are derived from a simplified simulation environment. Consequently, policy makers and regulators utilizing the ASAM can investigate advanced ancillary service design queries, such as comparing all-or-none vs. proportionall-or-none design choices. Ultimately, the validation of these findings against realistic market data and advanced market agent representations remains a crucial area for future research.

This study constrains the formation and dissipation timescales for vortices in both hemispheres, focusing on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), characterized by higher temperatures and increased hydrocarbon levels at millibar pressures. While the NPSV began forming in late northern spring, it lacked the distinct thermal and compositional contrasts observed at the south pole during its southern summer by the end of Cassini's observations, shortly after the northern summer solstice. The newly formed NPSV was defined by a steepening thermal gradient near $78^\circ$N. Its hexagonal boundary suggests that the Rossby wave responsible for Saturn's persistent polar hexagon—previously thought to remain in the troposphere—can impact stratospheric temperatures roughly 300 km above the cloud tops. We speculate that this wave was activated when the northern obliquity approached $26.7^\circ$, its maximum value. Cold air advection signaled the onset of NPSV formation and was rapidly followed by an increase in acetylene within the existing nitrogen haze, indicating gas-phase chemical kinetics that dictated the vortex's growth scale and speed. However, methane deposition on stratospheric haze particles, which relies on surface reactions, was not a limiting factor for NPSV formation. As the solstice was approached, the NPSV became thermally isolated, leading to adiabatic warming and the development of a strong rotational wind barrier at its boundary that halted its further expansion. Additionally, solar UV shielding by the ascending northern hemisphere caused photolytic source termination, resulting in depleted hydrocarbon concentrations that marked the NPSV's decay. These findings collectively illustrate the physical and chemical processes driving the polar stratospheric vortex's formation and decay on the red-giant planet.

Field theories with bounded derivatives can be modeled as sections of a 3-rank vector bundle over the configuration bundle, where the differentiation operator is defined by a morphism between two sub-bundles of the pullback bundle. We introduce the concept of a field equation morphism and show its equivalence with a connection on the symbol bundle; this connection can be viewed as a generalized Levi-Civita connection. When the configuration bundle forms a metric double vector bundle, the symbol bundle becomes a symplectical double vector bundle, and the associated Levi-Civita connection serves as a natural example of a metric connection on a symplectic double vector bundle. These findings are relevant to understanding the gauge theory of gravity within the framework of field theories involving bounded derivatives. The previous work by Gonzalez et al. to probe the molecular, atomic, and nuclear components of a sample. Although scattered light inherently contains both the amplitude and phase of the electromagnetic field, phase data is frequently discarded during standard intensity measurements. Nevertheless, phase information is often critical for reconstructing target details, a principle established in coherent x-ray imaging. This work presents a novel phase retrieval algorithm capable of recovering field phase data from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra. We demonstrate this technique using x-ray scattering from Mössbauer nuclei at a synchrotron facility. Access to phase data enables a superior reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental results—a level of precision unattainable through conventional methods. Consequently, our approach offers a powerful new tool for data analysis that will advance both x-ray quantum optics and synchrotron-based Mössbauer spectroscopy. These capabilities may eventually be applied at fourth-generation light sources to determine the phase of x-rays from stable Mössbauer isotopes, fostering innovation in both fields. We have developed a software package implementing this phase retrieval algorithm, which is accessible on the Internet of Things platform at http://things.fhi-berlin.mpg.de/messbauer. This software is available for download at https://github.com/schuetzph/retriever. The demonstrated phase retrieval method represents a significant advancement for x-ray quantum optics, enabling a rigorous quantitative assessment of quantum properties in macroscopic objects. Phases arise from time delays, providing access to dynamics across a broad spectrum of phenomena. This technique is particularly relevant for x-ray quantum information science, where novel coding schemes based on the holographic principle could one day allow data storage on objects as minuscule as a single atom. By storing information in both amplitude and phase, storage density would increase substantially. Our phase retrieval algorithm represents a promising step toward future x-ray coherent imaging systems capable of measuring the electromagnetic field phase at synchrotrons and fourth-generation sources. Such capabilities would unlock a range of novel applications, including characterizing single electrons or nuclei, enhancing medical imaging, or storing data on a single atom.
