The model represents fractures as $(d-1)$-dimensional interfaces within a $d$-dimensional domain, where $d$ equals 2 or 3. Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed {\it conductive}, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed {\it blocking}. Conductive fractures are modeled using a standard hybrid-dimensional interface approach assuming continuous pressure across the interface, whereas blocking fractures utilize a recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach that enforces continuity of the normal Darcy velocity component. A key innovation of this scheme is its ability to handle nonconforming meshes regarding blocking fractures, a capability enabled by the Dirac-$\delta$ formulation. Additionally, the numerical method yields locally conservative velocity approximations and generates a symmetric positive definite linear system defined solely on pressure degrees of freedom located at the mesh skeleton. Benchmark tests in both two and three dimensions demonstrate the method's performance, with results showing it to be highly competitive against existing literature approaches. The software implementation is available at https://github.com/vitens/DARCFLOW.

science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. Reproducible code is accessible at https://osf.io/y354c/.

Hypothesis testing serves as a cornerstone of cognitive science, where Bayes factors are frequently employed to quantify the evidence support for competing hypotheses and guide decisions. This paper outlines a methodology for evaluating the robustness of Bayes factors using utility functions and simulation-based approaches. Our findings reveal multiple sources of uncertainty in Bayes factors, suggesting that point estimates may be insufficient for evidence evaluation. We present a reproducible example from cognitive science demonstrating how this approach can optimize Bayes factor estimates and select the most reliable solution. Ultimately, our framework offers a general solution for the evidence assessment of Bayes factors in cognitive science. Reproducible code is available at https://osf.io/y354c/.

Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. It enables researchers to study markers from the perspective of their relations and assess models for natural language understanding using tasks such as discourse marker sense disambiguation and classification. Additionally, we demonstrate the DiscSense dataset's utility in constructing a simple model to predict semantic relations from discourse markers, achieving state-of-the-art results on three widely used datasets. We also illustrate how researchers can explore the relationship between semantics and pragmatics using this dataset. DiscSense provides a foundational resource for future research into automatic characterisation from corpus data, including studying the link between semantic tasks and discourse markers, as many tasks (such as sentiment analysis and title generation) currently lack the explicit inclusion of pragmatic information. We hope DiscSense facilitates investigations into the complex relationship between semantic and pragmatic information across various domains. Our dataset website is here: https://sites.google.com/view/discsense/home.

Abstract title sentence generation (ATSG) aims to create concise abstracts for research papers by leveraging their title and main content. Although several models have been developed for this purpose, they often struggle with factual accuracy and semantic diversity. To address these issues, we introduce a framework incorporating a contradiction detection module into the abstract generation process. Specifically, we integrate a diverse set of sentence representations to enhance semantic variety, and we employ a contradiction assessment method combining a classifier and a large language model (LLM) to ensure factual correctness. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed method outperforms baseline approaches on standard evaluation metrics and exhibits reduced semantic redundancy and increased factual accuracy. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/yzh0909

By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. Assuming the original objective function $f$ adheres to standard restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that the entire search space partitions into three distinct regions: (R1) a neighborhood around the target parameter where the objective is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (R2) areas surrounding all strict saddle points; and (R3) remaining regions characterized by large gradients. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first global landscape analysis of the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective under this specific Riemannian quotient geometry. These findings offer a complete geometric rationale for the enhanced performance of vanilla gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, under a weaker restricted strict convexity assumption, we establish that geodesic convexity holds in a neighborhood of local minimizers. Our proofs rely on a detailed landscape analysis of a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, serving as a pivotal intermediate step. Additionally, our conclusions rest on a standalone result identifying that the geodesic ball centered at $Y$ with a radius equal to one-third of $Y$'s least singular value forms a geodesically convex set under the Riemannian quotient metric.

Our introduced "social-learning" variants successfully establish this equilibrium, whereas "individual learning" versions fail to converge strategies to the Nash outcome. When players utilize "canonical co-evolutionary genetic algorithms," the game dynamics form an ergodic Markov Chain; consequently, we analyze simulation results using both specific methodologies and broader statistical tests. These analyses reveal that in the "social" scenario, states corresponding to Nash Equilibrium play are highly frequent within the chain's stationary distribution, while in the "individual learning" scenario, the equilibrium is never reached. Furthermore, the expected Hamming distance between limiting distribution states and the "NE state" is markedly smaller in the "social" case than in the "individual learning" case. We also estimate the time required for these algorithms to reach the Nash Equilibrium. Our findings indicate that structured environmental feedback, as seen in the "social" setup, is a critical factor for player success in repeated games. These results carry significant implications both theoretically and practically. On one hand, they offer insights into the complexity of establishing a Nash Equilibrium in such games and serve as a benchmark for evaluating learning algorithm performance. On the other hand, they provide evidence that an attacker can leverage a co-evolutionary genetic algorithm to identify the time of a second attack in a race condition attack game with constant attacks. We contrast this with recent studies showing that an adversary using a "individual learning" algorithm in the same game type cannot determine the time of the second attack with high probability. Additionally, in games featuring a Nash Equilibrium different from the "NE state," the expected Hamming distance in the stationary distribution is substantially higher for the "individual learning" algorithm compared to the "social" case. Finally, we discuss the relevance of these results to other fields, including the design of cryptographic protocols and the emergence of animal behaviors.

To ensure reliability in real-world deployments, these systems must remain robust against hardware soft errors that corrupt platform memory. Building on the proven effectiveness of activation clipping, this study constructs a preliminary safety case for classifier CNNs by showing that range supervision acts as a highly dependable fault detector and mitigator for relevant bit flips, specifically within an eight-exponent floating-point format. Additionally, we investigate novel, non-uniform range restriction techniques that successfully reduce the likelihood of silent data corruptions and uncorrectable errors. As a practical, safety-critical end-to-end demonstration, we apply our method to a vehicle classification task using ResNet-50 and the MIOVision traffic camera dataset. The quantitative results presented here can serve as a foundation for developing further, potentially more sophisticated, safety arguments for CNNs. Consequently, this work underscores the significance of, and provides techniques for, safety case construction in industry-relevant, end-to-end scenarios, rather than relying solely on abstract analysis, intermediate representation insights, or component-focused evaluations. Crucially, the actual selection of floating-point range restrictions serves as the core technical contribution of this paper.

Extending beyond simple word alignment, we implement multiple cluster-level alignments, ensuring that word clusters maintain consistent distributions across different languages. Our clustering strategy leverages three distinct signals: (1) neighboring words within monolingual embedding spaces, (2) character-level data, and (3) linguistic properties (such as apposition and locative suffixes) extracted from linguistic structure knowledge bases supporting thousands of languages. We propose a novel cluster-consistent correlational neural network designed to construct this common semantic space by aligning both individual words and clusters. Intrinsic evaluations on monolingual and multilingual QVEC tasks demonstrate that our method achieves significantly higher correlations with linguistic features compared to existing state-of-the-art multilingual embedding techniques. Furthermore, in an extrinsic evaluation using low-resource language name tagging, our approach yields an absolute F-score improvement of up to 24.5% over current state-of-the-art solutions. This confirms our hypothesis that rigorous cluster-consistent cross-lingual knowledge transfer results in a common semantic space that markedly enhances low-resource name tagging performance. The implemented cluster-consistent alignment approach offers a robust, automated, and largely unsupervised framework for creating common semantic spaces across multiple languages. The resulting multilingual common semantic space is publicly available to support researchers working on low-resource languages. Since its inception in 2018, the project has been recognized with best paper awards at both the Cross Language Processing Research Workshop (CLPR 2018) and the Main Conference of the International Working Group of Linguistic Data Interchange (WGLI 2018). We continue to refine the system by adding cluster alignments and evaluating performance on other extrinsic tasks, such as word tagging. Users can access the tool at https://w3s.uniparents.eu/ and researchers can download the data at https://uniparents.uniparents.eu/. Transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) spectra and integrated yields are derived across various centrality bins, ranging from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb collisions, characterized by final-state multiplicity. By examining both Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions, the study investigates systems with comparable charged-particle multiplicities but distinct initial geometrical eccentricities. A detailed comparison of spectral shapes between these two systems highlights an inverse relationship between radial and elliptic flow. Specifically, the results indicate that radial flow remains independent of the colliding system when normalized to similar charged-particle multiplicities. Regarding hadron chemistry, the previously noted smooth progression of particle ratios with multiplicity from small to large systems is also observed in Xe-Xe collisions. Furthermore, these findings confirm that two key characteristics of particle production at LHC energies apply to medium-sized nuclei: a proton-to-pion ratio lower than thermal model predictions and an increasing $\phi$-to-pion ratio as final-state multiplicity rises. To interpret these observations, we conducted simultaneous fits to spectra and yields using a relativistic ideal hydrodynamics model coupled with a thermal hadron gas model, adjusting parameters such as radial and elliptic flow, chemical potential, and temperature. The model successfully reproduces the data only when the cross-over phase boundary is incorporated into the equation of state. Additionally, the simultaneous fit to particle yields supports the inverse scaling of chemical and kinetic pressures. Overall, the results suggest that the late-stage evolution of Xe-Xe collisions shares significant similarities with Pb-Pb collisions. Introduction: The intersection of relativistic heavy-ion physics with nuclear and subnuclear physics lies in the discovery that the strong interaction cannot confine quarks and gluons at LHC energies. We present a summary of current knowledge regarding the properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) created in central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. This includes a brief overview of methods used to characterize the QGP's temperature and density, an analysis of the particle spectrum and their kinematic distributions, and an examination of particle correlations to identify collective phenomena. The study concludes with an assessment of how well the AMPT and URQMD simulations replicate the findings from the ALICE experiment.

9, Chile, particularly its capital Santiago, experienced extensive violence that resulted in the destruction of both public and private infrastructure. This study seeks to extend an epidemiological non-local model, previously effective in describing the 2005 French riots, to include the topological structure of Santiago's subway network and account for the observed spatial distribution of rioting. While the model accurately replicated the aggregated temporal progression of the disorders, it failed to reproduce the actual spatial pattern of activity in Santiago. This discrepancy is primarily due to the model's absence of a population displacement mechanism, a factor deemed essential for explaining the unrest episodes in the city. We also investigated the emergence of a critical threshold for the "frustration" parameter, an indicator of social instability, which varies based on the underlying subway network topology. The estimated threshold values for Santiago (approximately 0.18) and Paris (approximately 0.13) contrast with the threshold observed in a grid-like environment (approximately 0.25), underscoring the influence of network topology on the onset of collective behavior. Ultimately, this research demonstrates how key properties driving large-scale spatial separation during the Chilean riots can be captured through an adaptation of the Vicsek model to subway network geometry, thereby providing insights into the self-organization processes underlying such events. The findings suggest that preparing for future civil unrest requires an understanding of how individual behaviors interact with urban infrastructure to produce macroscopic outcomes. Consequently, the study concludes by proposing extensions to incorporate population mobility derived from mobile phone data and by outlining limitations regarding the model's application to cities lacking extensive subway networks.

Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. The authors present a new symbolic decision procedure for containment, utilizing Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives alongside Antimirov's rewriting technique. Furthermore, they extend Brzozowski's syntactic derivative operator into two generalized versions capable of operating on representable, potentially infinite character sets. Furthermore, the paper explores anti-derivatives as a complementary symbolic method for determining regular expression inequalities and presents an enhanced algorithm capable of detecting semantic equivalence between expressions. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the methodology's effectiveness, highlighting its potential to serve as a practical tool for analyzing semantic properties of extended regular expressions. Regular expressions serve as a universal language for defining text and tree patterns, with applications spanning compiler development, data cleaning, and security testing, particularly in static analysis for buffer overflows and format string vulnerabilities. While semantic equivalence and containment checks have been extensively studied for basic expressions (without intersection or complement), extending these problems to extended expressions remains challenging due to the lack of efficient automated decision procedures. The proposed symbolic algorithm addresses this by employing regular expression derivatives instead of automata conversions. Brzozowski's derivative operator, which represents the language of a modified expression $E_d[a]$ as $\bigvee_{\gamma \in \Sigma} (E[\gamma] \wedge \text{true})$, is generalized to handle representable, potentially infinite character sets $\mathcal{S}$ via the form $E[\mathcal{S}]$. This allows the containment problem $E_1 \subseteq E_2$ to be reformulated as the eliminable inequality $E_1[\mathcal{S}_1] \wedge \neg E_2[\mathcal{S}_2] \equiv \text{false}$, where $\mathcal{S}_1$ and $\mathcal{S}_2$ represent the differences between the expressions and the true character set. The narrative proceeds by detailing Brzozowski's expression derivatives, Brzozowski's decision algorithm for semantic equivalence, and provides references to alternative algorithms for semantic equivalence and containment.

. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes. Additionally, comparisons with internal memory attention models highlight the effectiveness of using external memory attention for learning-based VIO. Finally, we believe this paper opens up significant potential for applying external memory attention in VIO and other multimodal data fusion tasks. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Mohammadaminnia/External-Memory-Attention-VIO .

This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. Our findings reveal that SHOWS supports both "Fermi-arc" surface states and hinge states linking the projections of Weyl points. We successfully constructed this exotic SHOWS state theoretically and observed it experimentally in three-dimensional (3D) stacked electric circuits featuring honeycomb-kagome hybridizations and double-helix interlayer couplings. These results pave the way for achieving square-root topology within 3D solid-state systems. Furthermore, the concept of SHOWS may prove beneficial in various square-root hyper-dimensional systems, such as optical networks, neural computation architectures, and hyper-dimensional programming frameworks.

Semimetals are defined by the touching of bands at discrete points or lines, giving rise to surface or hinge states that run between these dimensional reductions of bulk topology. We extend this framework by defining a new class of semimetals termed SHOWS (showing surface/hinge states), which possesses cubic-nonlinear instead of quadratic dispersion relations. We demonstrate the existence of SHOWS both in photonic and electronic systems and confirm its square-root topology via the square-root of a Chern number. Specifically, in 3D SHOWS, pairs of hinge states connect SHOWS Weyl points, and the square-root of their Chern integers determines the SHOWS topology. Within 3D magnetic ferroelectrics, SHOWS emerges when domain walls intersect. Additionally, 2D SHOWS arises from square-root graphene dispersion at magnetic domain wall intersections in such materials. These results pave the way for manipulating square-root topology through symmetry breaking and external fields in 3D SHOWS, as well as providing a novel mechanism for square-root dispersion at defects or impurities in magnetic ferroelectrics. Furthermore, SHOWS may be realized in optical networks, neural computation platforms, and hyper-dimensional programming.

These teachers possess pre-training tasks and datasets that are distinct and mutually unknown. Our motivation arises from a current challenge in model sharing: despite significant investments in training large, capable networks, researchers and institutions often cannot share their pre-trained models due to privacy, security, or intellectual property concerns, even when they wish to contribute. The experimental results confirm that FedSA successfully amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models, achieving performance competitive with centralized baselines.

To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible entropy production during quenches driven by energy-momentum inflow from an infinite memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories. Our findings indicate that while the increase in both entropy and temperature—mandated by the Clausius inequality of classical thermodynamics—is necessary to avoid violating the QNEC in quenches involving transitions between thermal states with momentum (dual to BTZ geometries), it is not sufficient. For any arbitrary initial state, we establish lower and upper bounds on the increase of entropy (or temperature) given a fixed increase in temperature (or entropy). These results provide concrete examples of quantum lower and upper bounds on irreversible entropy production, confirming their existence as previously theorized. Additionally, we observe a monotonic behavior in the non-saturation of the QNEC over time following a quench and analytically derive their asymptotic values. For unitary evolution driven by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition involving two asymmetry monotones that ensures any state of a two-level system or a separable state of $N$ two-level systems can evolve unitarily into a distinguishable state with a fixed minimal error probability $\delta \in [0,1/2]$. The findings offer insights for analyzing the state preparation time of two-level systems and multi-qubit systems within various quantum information processing contexts, including adiabatic quantum computation, dynamical decoupling protocols, and driven two-level systems. quantum computing. To bring this technology to practical viability, it is essential to detect and mitigate material defects that cause decoherence. In this study, we employ terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy (SNOM) to examine the local dielectric characteristics and carrier densities of wet-etched aluminum resonators on silicon, a fundamental component of superconducting quantum processors. Leveraging a newly developed vector calibration method, we derive THz permittivity from spectroscopy conducted near the microwave feedline. By fitting the extracted permittivity to the Drude model, we determine that silicon within the etched channel exhibits a higher carrier concentration compared to buffer oxide-etched silicon, and we investigate post-processing techniques to lower these levels. Our findings demonstrate that near-field THz analysis offers a quantitative approach to evaluating and pinpointing potential loss mechanisms in quantum devices. Furthermore, this work introduces a rigorous calibration procedure for vector SNOM that enables high-resolution dielectric characterization in the THz frequency range.

Thermodynamic formalism provides an efficient framework for analyzing stochastic processes and their trajectories, particularly within the context of nonequilibrium dynamics and the search for emergent fluctuations. In this study, we apply this approach to a model of Brownian motion constrained within an asymmetric double-well potential driving an Amperes law like fluctuation. We calculate the large deviation function (LDF) associated with the time evolution of this fluctuation using both an analytical method based on THz spectroscopy and a numerical method via two-level system modeling. Our results indicate that a negative LDF corresponds to a minimum entropy state arising from spatial charge distribution fluctuations. Additionally, we determine that the LDF satisfies the symmetry breaking condition of the order parameter, which corresponds to the resonance frequency gap in the THz range. These discoveries offer a novel perspective on recent two-level system (TLS) phenomena observed in superconducting qubits. However, we also highlight that the simple model employed in this research has limitations when addressing real-world issues. To fully understand emergent TLS phenomena, one must consider a complex landscape of potential energy surfaces influenced by multiple degrees of freedom and external stresses. Our previous research utilized a VOLTAGE dependent LDF measured through TIME domain THz SPECTROSCOPY on device surface charge using a vector SNOM setup to characterize these complexities. The analysis of large deviation statistics through THz vector SNOM is expected to advance our understanding of TLS formation and their impact on qubit performance.

The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, encompassing questions that span multiple disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, beginning with volatile sources and sinks, and trace the path from the deep interior to the upper atmosphere, covering volcanic outgassing, surface-atmosphere interactions, and atmospheric escape. Additionally, we address complex historical factors, such as the impact of Late Accretion events, the connection between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the effects of geochemical and geodynamical feedback cycles on the atmosphere. Based on these elements, we formulate several plausible scenarios for Venus's history and their observable consequences, offering insights into how Venus might lose its atmosphere and become a barren, high-temperature, desiccated world resembling Venus. Finally, we propose future missions and scientific instruments capable of testing these hypotheses and advancing our understanding of Venus's atmospheric evolution and its links to the interior. These recommendations are particularly relevant for planetary scientists evaluating the habitability of exoplanets and the potential for life on other celestial bodies within our solar system.

Among these, the Hawkes process is particularly popular due to its ability to define the probability of new events based on the process's history. This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. Within a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we derive concentration rates for the posterior distribution regarding the parameters, assuming only mild conditions on the prior and the model. These findings also establish convergence rates for Bayesian estimators. Additionally, a key aspect of event-data modeling is reconstructing the interaction graph, or Granger connectivity graph. We demonstrate consistency guarantees for Bayesian approaches in estimating this structure, specifically proving that the posterior distribution remains consistent for the process's graph adjacency matrix and that a Bayesian estimator using an appropriate loss function achieves consistency. These results assume an infinite time series length; however, we also examine the scenario with finite data and establish convergence rates for the estimator distance to zero. The contributions are summarized as follows: (A) consistency (strong consistency) for the posterior distribution of parameters; (B) consistency for Granger connectivity; and (C) convergence rates for parameter estimates and Granger connectivity. The proposed results are illustrated through a numerical example and an analysis of Twitter data regarding earthquake magnitudes. Bayesian code for the case study is available at https://github.com/harunayipcel/TwitterEarthquake.

We introduce a plasma waveplate utilizing magneto-optical birefringence under a transverse magnetic field, designed to operate under ultra-high laser intensities. Uniquely, this device not only modifies the polarization state but also amplifies peak laser power. Numerical simulations demonstrate that a centimeter-scale waveplate can convert an initially linearly polarized pulse with 5 petawatts (PW) of peak power into a circularly polarized pulse exceeding 10 PW, achieving approximately 98% energy conversion efficiency for polarization transformation. The required thickness of the waveplate scales inversely with both the plasma electron density ($n_e$) and the square of the magnetic field ($B_0^2$); for conditions of $n_e=3\times 10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$ and $B_0=100$ T, the thickness is roughly 1 cm. This proposed plasma waveplate, alongside other plasma-based optical elements, is poised to be critical for the efficient deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. These advancements hold significant potential to revolutionize high-intensity laser-physics research, particularly in generating highly polarized electron positron pairs from laser collisions with solid targets and in producing all-optical electron positron linear accelerators from such collisions. Succeeding initial complexities, the evolution of this intermediate-mass supernova (iSN) steadily aligns with theoretical models for high-yield iSNe. Notably, the iSN's $^{56}$Co decay rate determines its luminosity across most of the observed timeframe. The source of energy heating the outer layers prior to the burst is identified as radioactive decay, and we precisely chart the production of $^{56}$Co through its photodissociation thresholds. Furthermore, our data offer some of the most accurate measurements to date of the wind characteristics of massive star progenitors leading to intermediate-mass explosions. Specifically, we determine a mass-loss rate of $\log~{\rm gsr} = -11.11 \pm 0.22$ with a wind velocity of $160 \pm 15$ km/s in the weeks following the explosion. Consequently, this iSN exhibits the most desiccated conditions to date for generating mass ejections that match the solar chemical composition of r-process elements. We pinpoint the exact optical $^{28}$Al dissociation rate in the iSN's atmosphere and quantify the residual amounts of various heavy elements based on their specific ionization states. Our findings demonstrate that a broad spectrum of r-process elements can be created via wind ejections across the range of explosion masses characteristic of iSNe. These results signify that iSNe are not merely submassive versions of core-collapse events, but represent a distinct explosive mechanism governed by specific progenitor properties. By utilizing the standardized physical indicators of SN~2020jfo, we can refine models of r-process nucleosynthesis and enhance our understanding of neutron-star merger events. Intermediate-mass explosions are intrinsically difficult to detect; however, with continued advancements in survey technology, we can improve our identification of these events and expand our sample of potential r-process nucleosynthesis laboratories. In this MuLE setup, a single LE mirror is partitioned into multiple segments, directing X-rays reflected from each segment onto one image sensor within a multiplexed arrangement. When each LE segment is oriented at a distinct rotation angle, the azimuthal rotation of the reconstructed cross-like image from a point source allows for the identification of the specific segment responsible for focusing the X-rays onto the imager. Utilizing a 30 cm focal length and 10 x 10 cm^2 LE segments, a field of view covering approximately 1 steradian can be achieved with 36 segments and just four imagers (each sized 10 x 10 cm^2). Ray tracing simulations were conducted to assess a nine-segment MuLE configuration. These simulations indicated that for a 1-minute exposure to a 10^3 counts s^-1 source, the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) for peak counting rate would remain within 30% of that achievable with a simple (non-MuLE) LE mirror. Furthermore, the simulations demonstrated that the nine segments could be successfully distinguished based on the direction of the cross shape in the observed images. Finally, we examined the feasibility of implementing a MuLE system with three components (N=3) for the Decameter-scale LE Mirror (dLEM), a large-scale LE mirror currently under development to detect transients from merging sub-solar mass black hole pairs. The findings from this study support the viability of MuLE optics for wide-field X-ray sky monitoring with good statistical accuracy and for detecting transients with counts rates around 10^3 counts s^-1 using relatively low-cost equipment. We encourage the exploration of MuLE optics for current LE projects, such as the dLEM, to expand the LE mirror's effective field of view, and for new initiatives aimed at observing astrophysical transients.

Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian formulation. Unlike the standard Eulerian approach, this formulation solves force balance equations to determine the positions of fluid elements mapped to grid points. Distinct from prior literature, we do not rely on the first integral of the Euler equation, which typically lacks a general analytic solution. For events involving neutron stars, the concurrent detection of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation offers significant potential to deepen our understanding of these phenomena and investigate the equation of state of dense matter. Urban physical meetings and social interactions are essential for economic progress and innovative thought, while also fostering community resilience and diverse social capital. Nevertheless, pandemic mobility constraints significantly lowered the diversity of urban encounters, raising questions about their effects on social diversity and the equity of opportunities for connection and exchange. -mass young stellar objects (HMYSOs) often fragment into multiple self-gravitating bodies, a process that may account for recently observed episodic accretion bursts. By applying a 1D code to resolve dynamics down to the stellar surface, we post-processed prior 3D simulation results. Our findings reveal that the burst-like deposition of material into the inner disc observed in 3D models does not invariably produce powerful accretion bursts; instead, only high-density clumps that have undergone collapse and crossed the inner computational boundary generate observable bursts. The complex physics of the inner disc significantly influences these bursts in four key ways: (1) While objects in standard turbulent viscosity discs may stall at migration traps a few astronomical units from the star, those in magnetised wind-driven discs can cross these traps to create bursts matching current observations. (2) Migrating objects can interact with and alter the thermal (hydrogen ionisation) instability of the inner disc, potentially causing longer-lasting, lower-luminosity bursts in HMYSOs. (3) If the central star is bloated by prior high-accretion episodes or if the migrating object is sufficiently dense, the outcome is a merger rather than a disc-mediated burst. (4) Disruption bursts from these objects may exceed the Eddington limit, driving episodic feedback on the HMYSO environment through powerful outflows. These conclusions are based on comparative models featuring identical initial conditions but varying physical complexities at the stellar surface. We urge future 3D simulation studies to incorporate realistic inner-disc physics to accurately model HMYSOs and their feedback mechanisms.

The primary objective is to characterize how uniform shear flow influences the modulation of weakly nonlinear, quasi-monochromatic surface gravity waves. By employing Hamiltonian transformation theory on the Hamiltonian formulation of the system, we derive a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation governing the temporal evolution of the wave envelope. Consistent with prior findings, our results indicate that the impact of uniform shear flow on the modulational instability of Stokes waves varies based on the flow's direction and magnitude, either enhancing or suppressing the instability. Furthermore, our approach offers a non-perturbative method to reconstruct surface elevation from the wave envelope, utilizing a Birkhoff normal form transformation to remove all non-resonant triads. The validity of this model is confirmed through comparisons with direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and with a recently developed Dysthe equation by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch (J. Fluid Mech. 855, 2018) addressing constant vorticity, demonstrating excellent agreement across a range of vorticity values. The study concludes by exploring the effect of uniform shear flow on the instability of surface gravity waves under a surface tension. Our research advances previous work by examining the response to counter-current flows and by considering the presence of surface tension. The significance of these discoveries lies in their potential relevance to the patchification of surface waves, as observed in contexts such as river plumes, atmospheric jet stream streaks, and marine grease patches. The findings underpin recent investigations into the universal mechanisms driving patchification under counter-current flows and are applicable to the stability analysis of surface currents with arbitrary velocity profiles. By applying Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we simulate the evolution of these fields to determine the Gaussian curvature of the parametric space, examining its behavior across phase transitions. The simulations reveal an unexpected phenomenon termed the \emph{curvature effect}, signifying a pronounced asymmetric geometric deformation within the parametric space triggered by substantial fluctuations in the system's entropy. This asymmetric pattern is linked to the onset of hysteresis, thereby establishing an intrinsic arrow of time within the system's dynamics. Furthermore, the study elucidates the underlying physical mechanisms driving this asymmetric curvature effect and its connection to hysteresis, highlighting the potential value of this perspective in investigating asymmetric phenomena within chemical and biological systems. Finally, the paper extends this analysis to a biomodel known as the phage--lambda life cycle model, demonstrating the applicability of the curvature effect and its role in determining the decision-making dynamics between the lytic and lysogenic states. The demonstrated genericity and physical significance of this phenomenon suggest its broad relevance to understanding decision-making processes in biological systems. Ultimately, this work introduces a novel and powerful computational and theoretical framework for analyzing stochastic complex systems, offering a new lens through which to view the thermodynamic states of such systems. The title reflects this focus, as the phage--lambda decision between its two life cycles serves as a prototypical model for stochastic complex systems.

$\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA), a robust alternative to conventional PCA, has gained significant popularity in recent years. To address this challenge, we introduce a proximal alternating linearized minimization method incorporating nonlinear extrapolation to solve the problem's two-block reformulation. We further demonstrate that the proposed algorithm converges at least linearly to a limiting critical point of the reformulated problem, which is proven to correspond to a critical point of the original problem provided a specific step size condition is met. Finally, numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the effectiveness of our approach. To facilitate future research, we have released our code alongside the paper at https://github.com/MohammadVaedenvish/L1-PCA.

Question Answering (QA) is a fundamental computational task with numerous real-world applications. We introduce a new dataset comprising 15,000 image-triplet questions and answers, where a question is defined as a pair selected from each of seven relationships (e.g., "more expensive than", "in front of") within a set of three images. We evaluate various ML models using this dataset and discover that even access to rich auxiliary image properties yields minimal performance gains, leading to the conclusion that these properties are implicitly encoded in multimodal representations. To investigate the semantic structure of these seven-triplet relationships, we apply a ML classifier to learn their meanings from the data. Our analysis of this learned structure reveals that the seven-triplet relationships are not atomic; they can be compositionally defined by a smaller set of abstract semantics (specifically, a 2x3 "bigram" matrix of semantics). This finding offers a fresh, evidence-based perspective on the image relationships included in our dataset and validates the compositional nature of visual semantics. The dataset is available for download and research at our project website: https://harvilliam.github.io/relqa/. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. Additionally, we propose a Mach-Zehnder arrangement to directly measure the discontinuity of the gravitational potential gradient at the superconductor's surface, arising from the expelled atomic mass. This approach builds upon the concept of measuring gravitational potential differences using the gradient of that potential rather than the potential itself. Ultimately, we illustrate how combining these two Mach-Zehnder measurements could facilitate the direct detection of gravitational magnetism manifested as the magnetic field of the superconductor's expelled mass. To realize this proposal experimentally, only minor modifications to standard atomic interferometry techniques are necessary. Additionally, this testing-magnet configuration may serve as a precise method for determining the magnetic susceptibility of superconductors. viewed as inefficient for SIMD high-performance computing (HPC), even though many critical HPC applications naturally possess an object-based structure. On SIMD accelerators like GPUs, this limitation stems primarily from memory allocation and access issues. Although a few libraries offer parallel memory allocation for accelerator devices, they all suffer from uncoalesced memory accesses.

We have identified a broad category of object-oriented programs, including many significant real-world applications, that can be efficiently executed on massively parallel SIMD accelerators. We term this category Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), as it expresses parallelism by executing a specific method across all instances of a given type.

To enable average programmers to utilize fast GPU programming for SMMO applications, we developed DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework. DynaSOAr comprises three core components: (1) a fully parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator; (2) a data layout Domain-Specific Language (DSL); and (3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. By controlling both memory allocation and access, DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization by adopting a Structure of Arrays (SoA) data layout and reduces memory fragmentation through the efficient management of free and allocated blocks using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps. Unlike other allocators, our design relies heavily on atomic operations, prioritizing overall application performance over individual kernel execution speed.

The data layout DSL simplifies memory access for programmers and minimizes conflicts during coalesced reads and writes. This access pattern also reduces write-overread conflicts, an innovation unique to our approach. Our do-all instruction, which underpins the parallel execution of methods for all object instances, reduces global synchronization to a single point per kernel, thereby maximizing parallelism.

We evaluated DynaSOAr's memory management, data layout DSL, and overall performance using C++ SMMO applications running on a GPU. Our results show that DynaSOAr performs at least as well as, and often better than, manually optimized "flat" global arrays. Specifically, we achieved a 1.55× speedup in one test case and a 1.22× speedup on average. In terms of memory, we reduce global memory bandwidth usage by 48% and decrease memory fragmentation from 100% (using standard new/delete) to 10%. These findings indicate that object-oriented programming can be made fast and efficient on current GPU architectures.

Through a detailed orbital decomposition of local densities of states, we examine the formation mechanisms of YSR states for an Mn adatom and two configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface, contrasting our theoretical outcomes with recent experimental data. Our results for a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer align well with the experimentally observed splitting of YSR states; however, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, the spin-orbit coupling proves insufficient to explain the experimentally observed splitting. Additionally, altering the relative orientation of magnetic moments within this dimer induces splitting and energy shifts of the YSR states, ultimately resulting in the emergence of a zero-bias peak for the deepest YSR state. We argue that this phenomenon arises from the reorganization of induced orbital currents on Nb atoms, which split the YSR states into pairs exhibiting symmetric behavior relative to the Fermi level. Finally, the exchange splitting between the $d_{\uparrow,z^2}$ and $d_{\downarrow,z^2}$ states drives the disappearance of the $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the antiferromagnetic dimer scenario. These insights are directly applicable to the interpretation of spectroscopic signals from magnetic adatoms and dimers on superconducting surfaces, thereby aiding in the identification of the quantum nature of YSR states. The computational strategy employed for analyzing YSR spectra is also suitable for investigating other properties of these systems, including local spin polarization on substrate atoms, the impact of an applied magnetic field, and the response to energy resolution limitations in experiments.

This paper addresses the question of determining the maximum value of $\lambda$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ guarantees a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor with a vertex set possessing an upper density of at least $\lambda$, for a given finite graph $F$. We establish a novel lower bound for this problem; for specific graphs $F$, including cliques and odd cycles, this bound is optimal as it aligns with a previously known upper bound. Furthermore, in the specific instance where $F$ is a triangle, we provide an explicit lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \approx 0.62203$, which surpasses the earlier best result of $3/5$. Alongside the referenced prior work, our findings confirm that the upper bound established by Montellat in 2020 is indeed optimal for all $F$. Additionally, we introduce a general method for constructing a specific type of 2-edge-colored complete graph with a vertex set of positive upper density that lacks a monochromatic $K_5$-factor. These results extend previous studies by Ferreyra and Montellat, as well as Cioabă and Montellat. Our approach relies on an explicit generalization of a construction by Rodl and Rucinski regarding infinite $K_p$-factors in Ramsey ultraproducts, alongside a novel application of an idea by Galesi concerning large independent sets in graphs with high minimum degree.

By employing an out-of-time-order correlator to measure the mass gap, we analyzed the impact of noise from amplitude damping and generalized Pauli decoherence channels on both qubit and qutrit systems. Our results indicate that for equivalent mass determination precision, qutrit simulations can withstand 10 to 100 times more gate noise than qubit simulations. Furthermore, we conclude that achieving 20% accuracy in the mass gap is feasible with qutrits in the near future but remains unattainable using qubits. This study serves as a proof of concept, demonstrating that qudits offer significant advantages for studying decohering quantum field theories in low dimensions, a capability that may soon be realized with existing quantum hardware. Quantum electrodynamics (QED) provides a fundamental framework for understanding interactions between charged matter and fields. While qutrits show promise for simulating $(1+1)$-dimensional Abelian Higgs models to within 20 percent accuracy in the mass gap, our standard fourth-order Taylor-striped local TSP algorithm requires approximately 2000 T-gates per TSP step for qutrits. Given that current qutrit devices typically sustain no more than 1000 T-gates before noise dominates, we developed a novel TSP algorithm utilizing fewer than 500 gates that maintains similar precision in the mass gap. We validate this new approach against the standard method and demonstrate its superior resilience to common qutrit noise models. This enhanced noise robustness arises because our algorithm employs a coherent basis change to diagonalize the kinetic term, thereby distributing noise effects more effectively. This study establishes a proof of concept for the efficient and robust simulation of QED and similar theories using qudits. Our source code is accessible online.

in the strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) regime has been established, yet their polarization status remained unreported, constraining potential applications. This study utilizes QED particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate electron-positron spin and photon polarization to examine a standard laser-solid configuration where an ultraintense linearly polarized laser strikes a foil target featuring a micrometer-scale preplasma. Our results indicate that when laser intensity surpasses $10^{24}~\rm W/\rm cm^2$ and positron yield becomes significant, the produced positrons exhibit clear polarization. Specifically, these polarized positrons can achieve a polarization degree exceeding 30% and a charge greater than 30 nC, with a flux of $10^{12}\,{\rm sr}^{-1}$. The degree of polarization varies with deflection angles, reaching up to 60% at specific energies and angles. This angular dependence stems from the asymmetrical laser fields experienced by positrons within the skin layer of the overdense plasma, where radiative spin-flip and radiation reaction are critical factors. This is the first direct evidence of positron polarization in laser-solid interactions, a phenomenon that can be optimized and is of significant importance for cutting-edge experiments, including precision tests of QED, time-reversal symmetry violations, and antimatter spectroscopy.

set $S \subseteq G$, the diameter $diam(G,S)$ denotes the smallest integer $n$ such that every element of $G$ can be expressed as a product of at most $n$ elements from $S$. In this work, assuming $|S|$ is bounded, we identify groups with polynomial diameter as those possessing a substantial abelian section near the top, specifically one whose size constitutes an exponential fraction of the total group order. This finding extends a significant result by Breuillard and Tointon. Consequently, groups exhibiting polynomial diameter are shown to contain a large nilpotent subgroup of class at most $2$ and to possess a high number of conjugacy classes. These conclusions align with and extend the main discoveries by Breuillard, Gerritssens, and "the authors" regarding groups with polynomial diameter. Furthermore, we provide an explicit bound for the diameter of general groups given the size of the second term in the lower central series of a maximal nilpotent subgroup, an result that is of interest independent of the polynomial diameter assumption. This bound is derived using techniques by Bishop and "the author", as well as estimates by Kuznetsov and "the authors" on the number of conjugacy classes in groups acting on Riemann surfaces with large genus. We also present a counterexample demonstrating that the assertion of polynomial diameter implies a bounded solvability class for groups with fixed $|S|$ is false. The proof of our main theorem relies heavily on quantitative versions of the a priori and a posteriori results by Breuillard and "the authors" concerning groups with many conjugacy classes. Additionally, we utilize recent findings by "the authors" on the uniform expansion of graphs of groups to establish that the specified fractional size of the abelian section is optimal. Finally, our approach yields several other results, including an improved lower bound for the number of conjugacy classes in groups with polynomial diameter in terms of $|S|$, and the existence of a bound for diameter in terms of this count and $|S|$ for groups satisfying the large conjugacy class condition, which is notably smaller than the general bound. An introduction is available in the source code repository. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/andreasconner/GroupsWithPolynomialDiameter .

The sensor's front-end utilizes a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to transform local temperature into two biasing currents, which subsequently determine two oscillation frequencies. The ratio of these frequencies corresponds directly to the absolute temperature. The back-end then converts this frequency ratio into a digital temperature code. Benefiting from its low-complexity architecture, the design offers a compact footprint, low power usage, and high accuracy across a broad temperature spectrum. Additionally, an embedded line regulation mechanism enables voltage scalability. Prototyped in 180nm CMOS, the sensor operates within a 0°C to 100°C detection range, supports a supply voltage from 0.6V to 1.8V, and occupies a minimal silicon area of 0.021mm². Experimental results from 20 test chips demonstrate competitive performance metrics, including a resolution of 0.24°C, an inaccuracy of ±1.4°C, a sampling rate of approximately 1.5kHz, and an energy consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion at 30°C.

cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud (designated as G28.37+0.07 or G28.34+0.06) classifies them into protostellar and starless groups based on their connection to molecular outflows. Statistical tests reveal that protostellar cores possess greater mass than starless cores, even when accounting for biases related to temperature and opacity. We propose that this mass disparity signifies core growth occurring after formation. Consequently, massive star formation may not necessarily originate from massive prestellar cores, contingent upon the rate of this mass accretion. The implications of this finding for the relationship between the core mass function and the stellar initial mass function require further investigation. Additionally, the average mass of protostellar cores in the Dragon IDL (approximately 3 times the solar mass) exceeds the minimum mass needed for a star of 1 solar mass to form on a free-fall timescale (around 2 times the solar mass). This suggests that in the Dragon IDL, protostellar cores may accrue mass too slowly to readily support massive star formation, or that such stars could utilize mass from surrounding areas. Ultimately, determining how massive stars form in various regions could help resolve the discrepancy between the core mass function and the stellar initial mass function at high masses. Statistical analysis indicates that the cores in the Dragon IDL are not primed for massive star formation, yet the IDL possesses sufficient mass to generate stars up to 50 solar masses without needing to accrete from external sources. Furthermore, we document three outflows among the surveyed starless cores, bringing the total count in this dark cloud to at least six. The presence of outflows in such massive, cold cores (T_dust approx 10 K) aligns with theoretical predictions regarding the drivers of star formation. These observations underscore the significance of identifying outflows to understand the actual mass available for star formation and to identify the most massive cores capable of forming stars.

Specifically, for the sphere ${\mathbb S}^{d-1} \subset {\mathbb R}^d$, the strict positive definiteness of a zonal function $f(\cos \theta)$ is governed by the signs of the coefficients in its expansion using Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$, where $\lambda=(d-2)/2$. While recent findings indicate that classical differentiation and integration preserve positive definiteness in this setting, these operations shift the space dimension in increments of two. This paper introduces operators for zonal functions on the sphere that maintain (strict) positive definiteness while transitioning between dimensions by steps of one. These fractional operators are specifically designed to act suitably on the Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$. Notably, a method to maintain positive definiteness during dimension changes was previously established for Fourier series on ${\mathbb R}^{d} // {\mathbb Z}^d$, encompassing the Bochner and Schoenberg theorems as special cases; we draw a comparison between this approach and the techniques used for zonal functions on spheres. The proposed fractional operators may also hold value in extending positive definite scattered data interpolation to zonal functions on ${\mathbb S}^{d-1}$. To achieve this, we first establish the (strict) complete monotonicity conditions required for a zonal function to be (strictly) positive definite, then derive formulas for the variations of its Gegenbauer series coefficients under differentiation, integration, and the new fractional operations. Our results include formulas for fractional differentiation and integration of zonal functions, which generalize previous findings on Gegenbauer coefficients to a fractional context. As an application, we revisit Schoenberg's example of positive definite zonal functions, generating a family of such functions indexed by a real parameter. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between these results and positive definiteness criteria for Fourier series via Herglotz' theorem. Finally, we extend our framework to zonal functions depending two variables $(\theta, \rho)$, which represent the geodesic distance and radial distance for points in the open unit ball ${\mathbb B}^d // {\mathbb S}^{d-1}$. \arxiv{1810.05205}

By integrating stress measurements with visual observations of various rough surfaces moving through dry liquid foams, we demonstrate the existence of three distinct friction regimes: slippage, stick-slip motion, and anchored soap films. Translation (NMT), directing the translation process by selectively attending to specific parts of the source sentence during the prediction of each target word. However, we observe that generating a target word relies not only on the source input but also heavily on previously generated target words, particularly distant ones that recurrent neural networks struggle to model effectively. To address this, we introduce a novel look-ahead attention mechanism designed to directly capture dependencies between target words. Additionally, we devise three integration patterns to incorporate this mechanism into conventional attention models. Experiments conducted on Chinese-to-English (NIST) and English-to-German (WMT) translation tasks demonstrate that our proposed look-ahead attention mechanism yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Social media has seen a surge in political discourse, with political figures actively utilizing platforms like Twitter to engage voters through direct communication. Despite the apparent utility of analyzing these interactions, the task is complicated by the sequential and often fragmented nature of messages sent across time. This study investigates the core challenge of modeling long-term dependencies within multi-turn source inputs for machine translation. We propose a novel look-ahead attention mechanism that captures long-range dependencies by directly modeling past target words. Experimental results on English-to-German (WMT 2019) and Chinese-to-English (NIST) translation show consistent performance gains when this mechanism is integrated into standard neural machine translation pipelines. The look-ahead attention mechanism is now freely available for public use and further research at the following link: https://github.com/ruibos95/LookAhead-Attention.

While recent studies have explored the application of machine translation (MT) for data annotation—specifically creating sentence-level alignments for semantic parsing—most existing approaches rely on sentence-pair attention mechanisms. These traditional methods are limited because they fail to adequately model long-term dependencies within multi-turn conversation contexts. To address this, we introduce a new look-ahead attention mechanism designed to capture long-range dependencies in sequential text for MT-based annotation. Our experiments indicate consistent performance improvements when this mechanism is used for MT-based annotation in dialog settings on the SemEval task. The look-ahead attention mechanism is openly accessible at this address: https://github.com/ruibos95/LookAhead-Attention.

Abramson and Parashar contend that a comparable divide exists between sophisticated computational technologies and increasingly demanding applications, necessitating a parallel field known as translational computer science. In this discipline, the intentional transition of research findings into large-scale practice becomes a primary research objective rather than a secondary consideration. Examining the evolution and deployment of grid computing from the mid-1990s through this lens reveals that a translational framework effectively elucidates both the technology's development and its impact. Specifically, the growth of grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit was facilitated by this translational methodology. Furthermore, the authors highlight key lessons derived from these experiences that can inform future translational computer science endeavors. Globus Corporation grants permission to reproduce this work in whole or in part in settings involving the development of educational materials or research. Translational computer science holds significant potential for addressing pressing challenges in areas such as climate modeling, genomic analysis, and national security. However, realizing this potential demands continued collaboration among researchers, engineers, end users, and infrastructure providers to create an environment where innovative work can emerge and mature. This computational paradigm can be adapted to other domains, including embedded systems, software engineering, and artificial intelligence. TranScriptome Assembler facilitates the assembly of high-quality de novo transcriptomes using RNA-Seq data, even for species lacking a reference genome. Its success was demonstrated on both simulated and experimental data, and it has been adopted as a default tool in the differential expression analysis package DESeq2. Our results indicate that TranScriptome Assembler can generate high-quality transcriptomes from as few as two or three deeply sequenced paired-end libraries.

Introducing unknown constituents into general relativity to account for galaxy and universe evolution remains contentious. The most recognized model is dark energy [1], typically represented by a homogeneous scalar field [2–8], though other formulations exist [9–14]. Additionally, the nature of dark energy is often probed via the equation of state parameter [15–20]. Despite two decades of investigation, its fundamental character remains unconfirmed [21–24].

An alternative approach involves dark fluid [25], which unites dark matter and dark energy into a single entity defined by an equation of state [27–32]. While this simplifies the universe into two components—baryonic matter and dark fluid—it renders the solution for universe evolution under general relativity underdetermined without specifying the equation of state. This freedom has led to various proposed dark fluid models [33–40]. However, the premise that dark matter and dark energy are distinct fundamental fields is widely supported by both theory

ays into invisible particles constrain light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter (DM). Utilizing low-energy effective field theories (EFTs) to model general neutrino interactions and Dirac fermion DM coupled to charm quarks, we conduct likelihood fits for individual neutrino and DM operators featuring distinct Lorentz structures and photon spectra for the process $J/\psi\to \gamma+{\rm invisible}$. We derive limits on decay branching fractions across various neutrino and DM scenarios, converting these into lower bounds on new energy scales. The strongest constraints on the energy scale for neutrino and DM EFTs are found to be 12.8 GeV and 11.6 GeV, respectively. Additionally, the purely invisible decay $J/\psi\to {\rm invisible}$ offers complementary constraints on effective operators, with energy scale bounds exceeding 100 GeV for dipole operators. We also determine limits on the DM-nucleon scattering cross section based on $J/\psi$ data. These invisible decay measurements are sensitive to light DM masses that remain unprobed by current direct detection experiments. Furthermore, the future Super Tau Charm Factory is projected to improve these limits by two orders of magnitude after a one-year run. We also explore the sensitivity to light DM properties at the next Large Hadron Collider (LHC) run and assess the ability of future high-luminosity $e^+e^-$ colliders to detect light DM through recoil electron spectra in $e^+e^-\to e^+ + {\rm missing}$. The results for other charmonium states are discussed, and the findings are compared with constraints from other processes. This work highlights that the STCF will significantly advance our understanding of interactions between the visible and dark sectors. This is especially pertinent to light DM, which is a primary candidate in neutrinoless double beta decay searches, LHC experiments, astrophysical missing energy observations, and short-base-length neutrino experiments.

**Keywords:** $J/\psi$ physics; sub-GeV dark matter; sterile neutrinos; effective field theory; STCF; LHC; high-luminosity $e^+e^-$ colliders.

Furthermore, we derive upper and lower bounds for $\mathbb{E}\left(\int_0^1 y \Lambda(t,\mathrm{d}y)ight)$, where $\Lambda$ is a measure associated with the excursion law of $S$ from zero; specifically, $\mathbb{E}(\Lambda([0,1], [0,\infty))) \sim 1/1.59439...$. Finally, we note that several of these conclusions remain valid even when the increments of $S$ are merely identically bounded. Several of these main conclusions are supported by numerical simulations. During the presentation, key intermediate findings are also highlighted. (IShTAR) serves as a specialized facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany, designed to study the interaction between ICRF waves and plasma. This platform enables the systematic investigation of ICRF heating mechanisms and associated plasma phenomena through the controlled variation of experimental parameters. Utilizing IShTAR, the maximum ion cyclotron resonance layer temperature has been raised for the first time to approximately 50% of the background plasma temperature. This achievement was made possible by implementing a novel scheme for generating sideband frequencies, a component crucial for sustaining resonance within a magnetically confined plasma. Concurrently, a significant discovery at IShTAR involves the formation of sideband cyclotron resonances, which offer a novel mechanism for ion cooling. These findings carry important implications for enhancing our comprehension of ICRF heating inefficiencies and other secondary plasma effects within magnetically confined fusion reactors. At IShTAR, sideband cyclotron resonances occur near the electron Larmor radius scale, marking the closest natural environment to the conditions anticipated in ITER for such interactions. In this study, we present the experimental evidence for sideband ion cyclotron resonance at IShTAR and determine their precise location using a simplified model of the ICRF antenna system. Furthermore, the potential cooling effect on ions via this mechanism is quantified, and potential implications for future large-scale tokamaks are assessed. IShTAR's capabilities for further exploring these phenomena are also discussed. At this advanced plasma test bed, the temperature of the ion cyclotron resonance layer can be precisely controlled by adjusting sideband frequency parameters; consequently, verifying the cooling signature experimentally represents a feasible future objective. Additionally, IShTAR can investigate the spatial distribution and temperature dependence of these sideband cyclotron resonances, thereby enhancing the accuracy of models designed for ITER-style tokamaks. The IShTAR experiment represents the first instance of observing sideband ion cyclotron resonances, and its findings align well with theoretical predictions. However, more sophisticated antenna models incorporating wave propagation effects are necessary to fully capture the experimental data. At ITER, sideband resonances will exist both in the electron beta-cyclotron resonance region and within the hydrogen cyclotron resonance zone. While the cooling impact is expected to be modest for electrons, it could be substantial for heavier ions like ITER's primary fuel components. In such scenarios, the proximity of sideband cyclotron resonances to the electron resonance region might exacerbate challenges related to neoclassical tearing

Nucleus segmentation technology is commonly employed to automate these tasks; however, training robust segmentation models remains challenging due to issues like nucleus adhesion, stacking, and excessive background fusion. Although recent approaches based on point annotation have significantly enhanced model performance, they still require experienced pathologists to provide the necessary annotations. By segmenting the grid into superstates, such as "rooms," the method establishes a dual-resolution decision-making system comprising local PEGs at the granular state level and an aggregated PEG at the superstate level. Due to their reduced state space size, both the local and aggregated games can be efficiently solved to reach a Nash equilibrium. To bridge these two levels of decision-making, the Nash values derived from the local PEGs serve as rewards for the aggregated game. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this hierarchical approach substantially lowers computational costs while preserving performance comparable to flat Nash policies during competition. lepton colliders operating above a few TeV function effectively as electroweak (EW) boson colliders, implying that EW bosons can be treated as constituents within high-energy leptons. Focusing on muon colliders, we re-examine the validity of $W$ and $Z$ parton distribution functions (PDFs) at leading order for $2\to n$ processes. We systematically analyze universal and quasi-universal power-law and logarithmic corrections that emerge when deriving (polarized) weak boson PDFs in the collinear limit. Furthermore, we survey numerous $2\to n$ processes at center-of-mass energies ranging from 2 to 30 TeV through polarized and unpolarized electroweak boson fusion and scattering. To facilitate this investigation, we present a public implementation of the Effective $W/Z$ and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations—collectively termed the Effective Vector Boson Approximation—within the Monte Carlo event generator \texttt{MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO}. This implementation establishes the foundation for creating matrix-element matching schemes that incorporate EW parton showers and renormalized EW PDFs. In support of this initiative, we also provide specific recommendations regarding the application of $W/Z$ PDFs. Additionally, to enhance our comprehension of the EW sector at center-of-mass energies exceeding 30 TeV, we urge the inclusion of EW boson fusion and scattering events involving three or more final-state bosons. These findings will directly facilitate the design of a muon collider and the planning of subsequent physics programs.

This paper presents an analysis of 34 years of Arecibo data regarding PSR B1133+16, yielding high-quality dynamic spectra and their corresponding scintillation arcs generated by screens along the line of sight. We identified six distinct screens responsible for these long-lasting arcs. Assuming the screens remained relatively stable over this period, we modeled variations in arc curvature across Earth's orbit to determine the position, orientation, and velocity of five of the six screens. Our most precise distance measurement places one screen at $5.46^{+0.54}_{-0.59}$ pc from Earth, which we associate with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble. Additionally, we observed one screen whose velocity does not match solar motion, suggesting it is not carried by the solar wind. Finally, we note the unexpected presence of multiple screens at nearly identical distances but with significantly different velocities relative to the Sun. These findings demonstrate that pulsar scintillation provides a robust method for discovering and measuring the properties of plasma screens located between the Earth and pulsars. The detection of six screens at approximately 5.46 pc suggests that fine structures within the local interstellar medium can substantially influence the solar system's determination of pulsar velocities along the line of sight.

While WN, a probabilistic autoregressive model utilizing stacked dilated convolutions, excels at high-fidelity audio synthesis, its reliance solely on data without prior audio knowledge hampers its ability to control pitch. Evaluations on single-tone sinusoids and speech demonstrate that the proposed method effectively handles unseen auxiliary $F_{0}$ values and improves speech generation through the cascaded design.
